speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week there was an ugly incident at the Tory leadership debate in Calgary which probably more than anything else shows how shallow the claim of politics of inclusion really is for that party.
Despite having paid admission Vickie Crowchild-Ab-erdeen, a native woman and a former Conservative member, was not only denied admission to the forum but was pushed up against the wall by PC security.
Tony Hall, a professor at the University of Lethbridge, was also refused entry. He was protesting the omission of aboriginal rights in NAFTA.
Yesterday MPs from all parties heard the chief of the Assembly of First Nations, Ovide Mercredi, testify before a committee that aboriginals "only know the politics of exclusion" and what is needed is "real access to the decision-making process of government".
What does this incident tell us? Perhaps the editorial board of The Edmonton Journal is correct in saying today: "Sometimes it looks as if the Conservatives are determined to lose the coming election".

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, May 7 will mark the nation-wide launch of the Hire a Student-Business Drive for Jobs campaign at a regional event site in each region of the country with the national kick-off ceremony taking place in Quebec City.
Employers and home owners almost anywhere in the country can call one of 400 student employment centres and ask for help in filling just about any kind of student employment opening. This student placement service of Employment and Immigration Canada is now celebrating its 25th anniversary.
Through the Business Drive for Jobs campaign four major business organizations have pledged to encourage their members to hire students. These business organizations are the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, the Retail Council of Canada and le Conseil du patronat du Quebec. As a result, many businesses will strike up a partnership with one of our student employment centres this summer.
Our next generation of workers is knocking on the door and I urge every employer to assist it.

Claude Jutras, executive vice-president of the Association des fabricants de meubles du Quebec, suspects an American company of dumping its products on the Canadian market which constitutes an unlawful trading practice. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make a critical comment on the issue of this federal government's minimum wage for people 17 years of age and older.
The federal minimum wage is below that of all the provinces and the states of Kentucky, Oklahoma, New York, Idaho, Montana, et cetera. Just how low is the federal minimum wage? Would you believe $4 an hour, Mr. Speaker?
The fact that most employees in Canada are governed by provincial standards and the collective bargaining process and there are very few individuals affected by the $4 an hour wage merely aggravates the situation. The fact that so few are affected does not negate the fact that this is exploitive and unjust and makes action more necessary and urgent.
The minister has indicated to me that his staff is reviewing the $4 an hour wage policy. I ask him to immediately pursue an Order in Council to rectify this totally unacceptable situation and grant these individuals an immediate increase.

speakerposition: subtopic

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, governments have to adapt to meet the realities of the 1990s, particularly in the area of fiscal restraint.
Governments must be creative and innovative if we are to meet the future demands of taxpayers. In this regard, I am pleased to inform the House that the Minister of Western Economic Diversification and the Alberta minister of federal and intergovernmental affairs yesterday announced the results of a review to reduce overlap and duplication between the Governments of Canada and Alberta.
While the task will be an ongoing one, progress has already been achieved. Both ministers have asked the public to assist a joint government effort to reduce overlap and duplication by providing ideas, advice and comments directly to their offices.
I applaud these efforts and encourage everyone to participate in this endeavour.

Parents and teachers will have to tell these children that the very Prime Minister who stood on the international stage to take credit for the UN convention on children has betrayed them yet again.
The Prime Minister will take $1 million out of funds that could be spent on hungry children for his final stray cat strut around the globe. The Prime Minister is content to have the red carpet rolled out for him abroad while children eat off the floor at home.
Perhaps his protege, the Minister of National Defence, will be able to cut the deficit because she knows how to take a trip without leaving her office.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans said in response to the Pearse-Larkin report that there would be no renewal of the aboriginal fisheries strategy this year unless there was a watershed agreement with respect to the Fraser River in particular.
Negotiations with the Americans on the Pacific salmon treaty have broken down. The fishermen are already suspicious about what the department is doing. Everybody involved in the industry is concerned that the department does not seem to be talking with any of the users, any of the people employed, or any of those who have any interest in the fishing industry in B.C.
We are heading into the next salmon season. It could be a very dangerous period if something is not done soon to get the people together, get them talking to each other, get them listening to each other, get them to agree on what is going to happen this year with respect to the watershed agreements if there are to be any, with respect to harvesting the resource, who will do the harvesting, and where it will be processed. All of these questions must be dealt with or we are going to be faced with a very serious period in the fishing industry in the province of British Columbia.

Mr. Speaker, sugar beets will be planted in our Manitoba sugar beet fields again this year. Sugar beet farmers have our federal Minister of Agriculture to thank for his dedication and strong leadership on this issue.
There are over 200 sugar beet growers in Manitoba and 100 permanent and 150 seasonal employees who
work at the Manitoba sugar factory in Winnipeg. These people can now breathe a sigh of relief that sugar beet farmers will be sowing their fields and harvesting their crops again this year. It is somewhat alarming that only at this late date, May 5, have sugar beet farmers been able to squeeze out of the province of Manitoba any level of support for their industry and for the large number of jobs that accompany it.
However our political leaders stood fast and strong to ensure that sugar beets will be planted this year. Once again, thanks to the Prime Minister and the federal Minister of Agriculture who have sweetened the pie for many.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today regarding a shipload of canola that arrived in Windsor, Ontario from France last week aboard the ship Federal Polaris. It was unloaded at a large elevator and oilseed crushing plant complex.
Southwestern Ontario soybean farmers and certainly western Canadian canola growers will be concerned about this 18,000 tonne shipment that could well undermine the existing oilseed price structure in Canada just at a time when Canadian farmers are preparing to plant the 1993 crop and market the last of the 1992 crop.
In view of the high subsidies paid to European farmers, will the government immediately report to the Canadian producers the level of subsidies provided for the growers of this product in Europe and undertake an investigation to ensure that this product is not being dumped into Canadian markets?

Mr. Speaker, we do not realize how fortunate we are to live in one of the finest countries in the world until we travel abroad and see what is happening in other countries around the world.
I rise today to make a statement on the question of a human rights violation in Vietnam. Vietnam is known to be oppressing its minorities, religious groups, freedom of expression, freedom of movement and so on.
I join with my colleagues in this House in calling on the Vietnamese government to respect human rights in Vietnam, to release all prisoners of conscience and to make sure that people in Vietnam have the right to freedom of movement, freedom of religion and the right to express themselves freely without any pressure or oppression.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the government about economic conditions in Quebec.
Last week the Minister of Finance tabled a budget that tells us that if the economy is allowed to take its course everything will be all right. However last month in Quebec another 4,000 families became welfare recipients, so that now the total number of people on welfare in Quebec is 750,000.
If the minister's economic policies are as effective as he says they are, why is the number of welfare recipients in Quebec increasing at such an alarming rate?
May 5, 1993

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as the hon. Leader of the Opposition knows, we have been through a very difficult and long recession which has not only affected Canada but has affected all the industrial economies of the world and particularly the G-7 industrial economies.
I think the hon. member would also be well aware of the fact that at the present time four of the seven G-7 countries have double digit unemployment. With the exception of Canada and the United States, the growth potential does not look promising.
Growth seems to be reoccurring in the North American market, but I know that just recently there have been some rather disturbing figures coming out of the United States. I think that may be of a short-term nature.
The fact still remains that Canada and the United States are poised to have the best rate of growth in 1993-94 and Canada will have the best rate of growth in 1994 of the G-7 countries as outlined by the IMF and the OECD.
Furthermore, according to OECD figures Canada will have the best rate of job creation at 2.3 per cent this year and 2.6 per cent next year.

At this very moment Montrealers are staging a sit-in at the campaign office of the Minister of National Defence and asking the minister to drop her helicopter program. According to them she should get her priorities straight because the cost of a single helicopter would provide 2,500 housing units for needy people in Montreal.
Since the Minister of National Defence refuses to listen to representations by opposition members urging her to abolish a totally unacceptable program, would the minister at least listen to the poor in Montreal?

Until we get some clarification from the Liberals about whether they are prepared to engage in those services to serve Canadians, it is very difficult to have an argument about costs.

The Liberal approach to costs is an absolute waste of funds, and I think the people of Montreal realize this.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister responsible for the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation. It seems obvious to me that we are going nowhere with the Minister of Defence.

I would therefore ask the minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing to intervene as soon as possible to save the social housing and co-operative housing program in Canada. Not only did the Government of Canada always assume its responsibilities for this in the past, but we now have a government which is violating this basic right to suitable, decent housing.
I would therefore ask the minister what he intends to do to ensure that the Government of Canada will continue to fund and subsidize social housing and co-operative housing for the poor and the most disadvantaged in our society.

Over the next five years we will be spending over $10 billion on social housing. Right now there are 652,000 units being helped under this program. We have looked after people who are handicapped, those most in need. He knows that under the budgetary constraints we have to seek new ways to be innovative to fund social housing
which we are doing. We are now able to borrow directly and pass the subsidy on. We are saving a considerable amount of money that way.
The member can be sure that we will continue to play a very constructive role in social housing and to continue to meet our responsibilities.

According to what we have been told by CMHC, the government is forcing CMHC to abandon its traditional responsibility in social housing and in co-operative housing.
For helicopters.

Yes, some of us say for helicopters. I want to know what the minister will do about this: The government is now asking CMHC to increase what those low-income people have to pay.

How can the minister accept increasing the rent paid by tenants of social housing to 30 per cent of their income? Is the minister sensitive to poverty? Will he ask the Minister of Finance to review this completely unacceptable directive to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation?

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
Once again it is clear that Canadians have expressed their view that unemployment is the issue of major concern to Canadians across this country. Such a result would only come as a surprise to a government that has ignored unemployment in this country and watched it increase without bringing in any kind of plan to address severe degrees of unemployment in this country. The European Community, Japan and the United States have all brought in jobs plans.
While there are only a couple of months left in this House, the Minister of Finance still has time to bring in a jobs plan for Canadians to give Canadians hope. Will he do that?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in The Financial Post of May 1, there was the headline "GDP climbs back to strength: Economy returns to levels seen before the recession". This is very encouraging news.
Mr. Earl Sweet, assistant chief economist of the Royal Bank of Canada, said and I quote: "The fundamentals are beginning to look positive now. We are on target for growth up to 3.5 per cent for 1993 as a whole. Contributing to that growth are hefty gains in productivity, substantial job creation and a booming export market".
I agree with that observation. The data that is coming out clearly confirms it. I think it is in large part due to the initiatives that we took in the February budget of 1992, amplified in the December statement which has provided for investments in people, in capital, in infrastructure, in job training and skills upgrading and indeed in small business.
Mr. Speaker, the reality is that every day we see more and more lay-offs. Tomorrow we are going to see 300 workers being laid off at the GM plant in Scarborough.
It is 3,000.

Sorry, 3,000 workers are being laid off in Scarborough. These are workers who have been

productive and who are highly skilled. Today a survey of 5,000 manufacturers indicates that they foresee increased productivity but fewer jobs.
Since this government has been in power, its economics have resulted in the real income of Canadian families being at the level of 1976 and yet the government continues to talk about a jobless recovery. How can there be a recovery without jobs?
I want to ask the minister: Why is the government prepared to accept a jobless recovery? Why will it not bring in a plan for jobs and get Canadians back working?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we on this side of the House, the government, have said no such thing. Since August there have been 202,000 full-time jobs created. There were 48,000 new jobs created last week and with the growth numbers we expect that to continue.
The hon. member takes great pleasure in outlining the number of people who have been dislocated or laid off. I would hope in her consultations with the Rae government in Ontario that she encourages them to take steps not only to reduce the deficit but to bolster growth. I would hope, above all else, they do not attempt to fight the deficit on the backs of the taxpayers of Ontario because that would kill any semblance of recovery that is now starting to occur.

I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I will also mention, the minister will be happy to know, that 85 per cent of the new jobs created in Canada have been created in Ontario. I am sure the minister is pleased about that.
Where?

Mr. Speaker, 71 per cent of Canadians also ask the government to increase taxes on the rich and on profitable companies. The consensus is that this would be a very good way to reduce the deficit. Why does the government choose to ignore this source of revenue? Is it because the rich are the financial supporters, friends and members of the Conservative Party?

May 5, 1993

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of National Defence.
As events unfold in Bosnia the situation of our troops there continues to be precarious. The commander of our Canadian forces said yesterday that peacekeepers could be targeted if there were air strikes. Yet an attempt to get any mandate or clarification of the role has been stonewalled by this government.
For the last month officials of the Department of External Affairs have refused to appear before the committee on request of the chairman for the last four weeks to give any kind of briefing because they say it is too risky and dangerous.
If the situation is so risky and dangerous in Bosnia and our troops are in this precarious position, why is Parliament not being informed? Can the minister tell us exactly when the government will present a clear, coherent assessment of the position and role of our troops in Bosnia and what steps are being taken to ensure their safety and security?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member knows, because it has been said in this House by myself, by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and by the Prime Minister, that the safety of our troops in Bosnia is our highest priority. Contingency plans are in place in order to ensure that safety.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs is in Sarajevo today. She was in Croatia yesterday and Monday. She will be returning to Ottawa and will be appearing before the standing committee in order to discuss the situation with members of Parliament as soon as she returns.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the minister another question.
The Prime Minister has committed to the Secretary-General that we are prepared to send more troops to Bosnia and perhaps our troops will stay longer in Somalia. However the Minister of National Defence has cut ground troops by 25 per cent, is committing 50 per cent reservists to provide replacement troops in Yugoslavia, and is saying that without new money there can be no further peacekeeping commitments.
How are we going to ensure that our new troops, the replacement troops, the additional troops, are properly prepared and equipped? What changes in defence spending is the minister prepared to make to meet our growing peacekeeping commitments?
Is it not time for the minister to realize that she should be cancelling the helicopter project so that we can meet the peacekeeping commitments the world expects us to make?

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is very interesting. The hon. member would like us to jeopar-
May 5, 1993

dize our capacity to patrol our own coasts, to perform search and rescue operations, and to protect Canadian lives at the expense of peacekeeping operations.
We now have 10 per cent of the world's peacekeepers. Our commitment around the world in 15 locations is very considerable. What the Prime Minister said was that Canada has responded in the past and would carefully examine any request for further assistance from the Secretary-General. We are now in the process of looking at a variety of ways in which we might respond or contribute to a plan to enforce and monitor the Vance-Owen plan if it is accepted by the Bosnian Serbs and if it becomes the basis for peace in Bosnia.
There is a variety of ways we can do it that does not necessarily involve ground forces. I will be appearing before the standing committee after Question Period today in the discussion of estimates and I would be delighted to expand at length on our proposal. I will be there with officials of the Department of National Defence. I would be very pleased to respond in detail to the hon. member's question in a way that is not acceptable in the context of Question Period.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the Minister of National Defence whose office is presently being occupied by 100 demonstrators concerned with social housing.
Three weeks ago the president of Agusta, one of the companies responsible for producing the EH-101 helicopters, was brought up on charges of bribery. We now have new evidence that corruption charges have spread to Belgium where it has been revealed that Agusta is being investigated on more corruption charges involving another helicopter program.
Given the seriousness of these charges, will the minister do the honourable thing and cancel this helicopter contract which is costing taxpayers $5.8 billion? I remind the minister these are not search and rescue helicopters. They are to search for Soviet submarines which are no longer there.

some training in the law and learn some fundamental principles of unsubstantiated allegations.

speakeroldname: Hon. Kim Campbell (Minister of National Defence and Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe the Secretary of State for External Affairs has commented that troops that would be used to enforce or secure the Vance-Owen plan would be under United Nations command and control. I am not in a position to indicate specifically what we would be offering because we have not seen a request from the United Nations.
When the United Nations engages in a military activity such as the peacekeeping plan, it sets out a list of its requirements which is circulated to countries. Those countries then see what they have available that they could add to the contribution.
The hon. member will know we now have 2,400 ground troops in the former Yugoslavia, half in Croatia and half in Bosnia. We are now in the process of rotating the second RCR to be replaced by the 22nd Regiment. We are in the process of bringing home some troops. We normally would give them at least 12 months in Canada before sending them abroad again.

This bill would allow the Secretary of State to establish a system of national scholastic achievement tests in consultation with provincial ministers of education. Students at certain school levels would be allowed on a voluntary basis to take these tests. Results would be disclosed to the students but the Secretary of State would make results public as statistical data.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader

They know that when this trade deal is signed and in place, when it passes through this Parliament and through the parliaments of the United States and Mexico, it will be as the U.S. candidate Ross Perot indicated. We will hear massive flushing and sucking sounds as the jobs are sucked and flushed down into the southern United States and northern Mexico.
We will hear one huge, sucking, flushing sound because this government is signing us into a deal that will not benefit Canadians generally. It will benefit the transnational corporations. The champagne corks will be popping on Wall Street. They will be popping on Howe Street in Vancouver and on Bay Street because the beneficiaries are the corporation owners. piece of paper. This symbolizes what we as New Democrats believe is the most appropriate way to handle this legislation and that is to tear it up piece by piece and not proceed with it.
The minister of trade is here. I respect him as a person. I respect him as an individual. But can he honestly say as a parliamentarian who has sat on this side in opposition for many years that it is appropriate with this legislation at the second reading stage, where we discuss the principle of this bill, to allow less than four hours of debate in this House of Commons?

It is unheard of in Canadian history that legislation of this importance would receive less than four hours of debate. The people of Canada might have figured out what this trade deal was all about.
Listen to what my friends across the way in the Conservative Party said a few years ago. When the Liberals were over there they acted like the Conservatives do today. They brought in closure on a regular basis. As a matter of fact, in 1980 the Prime Minister brought in closure on the Constitution. Your words have come back to haunt you.
The worm has turned.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader
speechtext:

We should not be surprised that this government wants to muzzle Parliament. We have heard the ring of jackboots around this place ever since the government members were elected back in 1984. Time and time again the stomping of jackboots in this place echoed throughout the halls of Parliament making a mockery out of this institution.
No wonder Canadians have given up because they know the government members do not listen to Canadians at all. They have their minds set on what they want to do. They have a responsibility to introduce legislation that will assist their wealthy corporate pals. That is what it is all about; it is the corporate Conservative agenda. It is called deregulation; it is called privatization; it is called downsizing; it is called laying off public servants. It is called all of those things and the cornerstone of that Tory corporate agenda is free trade. Who decides on the future of Canada? The corporate leaders decide and not even in Canada but in Hong Kong, Texas, New York, Los Angeles and Frankfurt. That is where the decisions are being made.
I have a book called Location U.S.A.. There are pages and pages of various states and cities saying: "Come to our state, here we do not allow unions," or "here it is a 'right to work' legislation," or "here there are very low minimum wages". It just goes on and on, seducing Canadian corporate owners into taking their operations down into Tennessee or Louisiana.
There was an example today in the press. We are tying ourselves into the economy in the United States. Does the minister of trade ever read the papers? Today it says that the United States figures show the recovery in the United States is slowing. We are tying our future to an

economy that is falling down. We are putting all our eggs into one basket and this government is asking the people of Canada to buy a pig in a poke. Why are we being asked to buy a pig in a poke?

One of these was raw logs. Those involved with the forest industry should not feel that because raw logs are mentioned as an exemption that this is going to safeguard their jobs, the mills or manufacturing plants. It does not take much to slap off four sides of a log and send that timber down to the United States. Will it now be sent down to northern Mexico where the employees are paid 60 cents an hour? Is that where it is going to be sent?
I will mention another exemption. It is unprocessed fish for the east coast of Canada. What about the unprocessed fish on the west coast of Canada? Why did the minister not ensure that that was protected so that those Canadian fish caught off our west coast are processed in Canada? Why should we be providing jobs for Americans or Mexicans? Those are our fish and those are our resources.
I want to ask my friend again. He is going to have a chance to speak and we will be listening very carefully. One of the very first things that our Prime Minister did when he was elected was to go down to New York to say: "Just in case anybody does not quite know, our country is now for sale to anybody. It is for sale virtually to the lowest bidder. Our country is for sale. Everything is for sale. All our resources are for sale. We are not going to ask these irritating questions about what value this will be for Canada. No, we are not going to do that. We are going to put Investment Canada into place to facilitate the takeover of our economy by foreigners".
That is what this government did. The idea is that the more foreigners who are making decisions about our future then the better it is. That is an odd way to think about the future of Canada.
That is not the New Democratic Party way. That is why we are tearing up this agreement page by page. We think this is not in the best interests of our country. It is not in the best interests of Canadians now or in the future. This as our economic constitution is how we believe we should proceed.
I want to ask my friend, the Minister for International Trade, to explain when he stands up why his government refused to include water as an exempt category.
Water is the only natural resource in this country that the Americans cannot just walk in and take over. It is the only resource that they just cannot walk in and buy at will. All the others are available for them.
Having brought this to the minister's attention back in the FTA when he had a chance to negotiate NAFTA, why did the minister not place water in there as an exempt category? He knows full well that that is what the Americans want. That is what they want. They want access to our fresh water. The Americans want to buy our lakes and rivers to feed their sloppy, wasteful habits in the southwestern United States and northern Mexico. That is what they want. He also knows that he is putting Canadian workers, in terms of their futures, in jeopardy.
I would ask this of the Minister of Finance who is a wise financier. He knows a good deal when he sees one, particularly for his corporate friends. He has a choice for the future. I hope he will respond to this when he has a chance to say a few words. He can pay his employees in Canada a decent wage, say $18 or $19 an hour. Under NAFTA he can go down into the northern tier of the United States and pay $12 an hour or he can go down into Tennessee, Mississippi, Louisiana, Texas and Arizona and pay $6.50 an hour. That is for the same type of qualification, the same expertise, the same education and the same training.
This is the gem. This document is now going to allow those same corporations to go down into northern Mexico and pay their employees 60 cents an hour.
My friend wants to maximize his profits and now has the ability to locate anywhere in continental North America. He knows that that Mexican border is only 48 hours by truck to anywhere along the most populated part of Canada and a lot less time to the markets in the United States. Say he is paying his workers $18 an hour.

This has been a very substantial process of consultation. It arises out of a consultation in 1985 when we were
asking people from across the country about entering into a free trade agreement with the United States. We asked: What do you want to see in this agreement and how should we manage ourselves as we go through this process?
One of the recurring themes was to have a formal, structured mechanism on an ongoing basis whereby people who had an interest or those representing interest groups would be able to feed these ideas into the process and engage in a dialogue with the negotiators. In that way they could have a real impact on the outcome of the negotiations.
Out of this flowed the process that we have now, which is the SAGFE-ITAC process. This has resulted in the SAGITs, Sectoral Advisory Groups on International Trade, which represent a range of industries, and I will give some examples in a minute, and have the responsibility of representing their sectoral and industry interests in the negotiations and providing ongoing advice on trade policy, trade development and other matters relating to trade. ITAC, the International Trade Advisory Committee, is an umbrella committee. It represents the chairmen of the SAGIT groups, but it also represents a number of other people from business, labour, and academia who are also feeding into the process.
These groups address issues directly related to the free trade agreement, then the Uruguay round and now the NAFTA. More recently we have engaged these people in a dialogue on the ongoing trade policy objectives that the Government of Canada should be following in the years ahead. This has been the main channel for consultations and direct involvement in the process.
I should also say that the process has been broader than that, with the prosperity initiative that started about six months or so prior to the completion of the NAFTA. This was a process that involved thousands of people across the country as well as industry groups on a broad range of issues. It gave people an opportunity during that time to influence the direction of the NAFTA negotiations.
If my colleagues opposite would read the comments of the steering committee on the prosperity initiative they would see how important international trade matters are. There is a broad process here. We now have 311

We in the
Official Opposition support the statement in the resolution before us today that would condemn the government for the stifling of debate through the misuse of closure by the enforcement of time allocation on NAFTA.
We came to this House believing this was a serious motion and one which carried our support. However, in place of a serious discussion we have once more been treated by the NDP to a footling, puerile and insubstantial discussion of what is in fact a very serious issue. We have also seen this little piece de theatre this afternoon which surely contributes nothing to Canadians' understanding of the debate we are now undertaking and, behind that, of the purpose and the impact of the North American free trade agreement.
We would support the motion before the House. We have seldom succeeded in having any impact in our continual and consistent urging for full discussion of
NAFTA. We nevertheless have repeatedly called for extensive or indeed exhaustive national debate on all aspects of the North American free trade agreement. We stressed in particular the need for full public participation of Canadians in this important process.
Let me quote for example from the Liberal Party's statement in the 1991 report on the North American free trade agreement by the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade. In that report we emphasized that: "The continuing consultation with Parliament and the Canadian people is a prerequisite to arriving at trade policy that reflects Canada's long-term interests".
To ensure that that full debate was pursued we in the trade subcommittee back in November 1992 supported wide-ranging consultation, not merely here in Ottawa but across the country.
At that time we put forward proposals to visit a large number of Canadian cities right across Canada. The response of the budget committee was unfortunately to endorse a truncated series of visits.
We accepted that knowing full well that if we did not accept the offer of the budget committee before Christmas we would have delayed the whole process until after Christmas when the question would have to be reopened.
What did the NDP do in those circumstances? The NDP opposed even the money that was allocated for visits to some of the major cities of Canada and chose instead to attempt to block any such consultation until such time as the budgetary allocation was made for a more extensive cross-country tour by the committee.
The result of that stance by the NDP would have been that we would have had no consultations prior to Christmas. We would have had no discussions in some of the major cities of Canada. It would have, in fact, prevented the beginning of even the truncated debate that we have had on NAFTA.
Similarly, in December 1992 we wrote to the chairman of the subcommittee on international trade. In light of the fact that we had been given budgetary allocations only for a limited amount of hearings, we proposed that in the new year the hearings could begin again with yet a much larger list of cities to be visited in every province and territory of our country.

We urged that hearings should be held in Saskatchewan, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Newfoundland, Yukon and the Northwest Territories as well as in the cities of Toronto and Montreal and indeed in a number of other cities in Canada, such as Hamilton. side agreements-the parallel accords as they are called-on the environmental and labour standards.

This government in its single-minded pursuit to get this legislation through the House of Commons is tying Canada's hands. It is leaving us little choice but to accept whatever the United States should decide is in its national interest, not in Canada's or Mexico's national interest, but in its own national interest in these and other important areas.
As the minister pointed out it remains technically true that even after third reading the government can still withhold proclamation of its legislation. Politically such a
step would be fraught with difficulties as the government itself surely must know.
The Liberal opposition has supported today's motion but it should be stressed that there is a critical distinction between the Liberal's and the NDP's position relative to the debate on NAFTA. The Liberal Party has a serious policy on trade and the NDP has no policy at all.
I am ready to debate that question and not engage in this little piece de theatre of tearing up papers and throwing them on the floor.
It is setting a bad example for children.

From the beginning the NDP members have rejected any idea of freer hemispheric trade. They condemned NAFTA long before its terms were negotiated and remain committed beyond that to abolishing the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement outright.
Their opposition is so blind and unrealistic. Where are they? What planet do they live on that they could move a motion in December that this House reject any North American free trade agreement? Is this NDP party so protectionist, so committed to building walls around Canada instead of enabling Canadians to participate in a new global economy that it can say it rejects any free trade in North America?
If that is its position then of course it is understandable why it does not participate in a serious debate, why it does not attend committee hearings and why in November and again in January it did not support broadly based consultations across our country?
By contrast, early in the process the Liberal Party set forth a number of ways in which the evolving North American trade relationship needs to be developed if we are to promote a truly liberalized trading agreement which implicitly recognizes the critical linkages. I want to stress that the Liberal Party recognizes the critical linkages between trade and economic activity on the one hand and environmental and labour concerns on the other.
Liberal Party members accepted Canada's participation in the NAFTA negotiations once Canada was a member of the U.S.-Canada Free Trade Agreement to take the opportunity to correct major shortcomings in the original U.S.-Canada free trade agreement, to
May 5, 1993

support what was in effect the renegotiation of that agreement and to ensure that Canada played a much more active role in shaping the evolution of North American trading relations.
We called for much tougher environmental standards. We called for much tougher labour standards. We called for those tougher labour and environmental standards back in 1991 when we first stated our position in a report of the standing committee. We called for an accession clause to make it easier for other countries to join the trading arrangement and thus expand Canada's free trade options beyond the United States.
Most important of all, we called for the inclusion of a subsidies and anti-dumping code which would put an end to the kind of trade harassment that has been eroding the so-called free trade environment between Canada and the United States. It would have introduced a desperately needed degree of predictability into our entry into the yet untested waters of a North American free trade agreement. A subsidies and anti-dumping code would have provided the Canadian people with a far greater degree of assurance than they can receive from the present North American free trade agreement.
Only the most sanguine among us would argue that the Canada-U.S. free trade agreement has lived up to the promises that this government so extravagantly made in 1988. I am not referring of course to the hundreds of thousands of jobs we were promised would emerge from such an agreement. I refer specifically to the fact that the central justification offered for the U.S.-Canada free trade agreement was secure access to the U.S. market in the face of what was seen as rising U.S. protectionism.
Despite the government's claims about the U.S.-Can-ada free trade agreement and now the North American free trade agreement, a whole series of trade disputes have arisen, from Honda automobiles to lumber. They have demonstrated just how tenuous that so-called secure access really is.
In some respects the North American free trade agreement did represent an improvement on the original free trade agreement, perhaps not a very difficult task. One of the major achievements is the access clause,

which I have already noted. It provides an opportunity for the development of a new and deeper level of a world trading order, a sort of GATT-plus if you wish in the western hemisphere. I will conclude this discussion now by merely recognizing that the NDP, in offering this motion today, had an opportunity to seriously address trade questions that confront every Canadian. In acting in this frivolous and superficial way on major issues, it has chosen a route that leads to sterility and rejection of everything. It leaves Canadians with no option but to develop a wall around themselves and opt out of the global world. We must all define, accept, challenge and take up the opportunity and ensure that all Canadians benefit from it.

I know the hon. member for Etobicoke North participated in the free trade agreement debate in 1988. I would like to know whether he was a party and privy to the allegations that the free trade agreement then, in terms of its perception would destroy sovereignty, attack Canadian sovereignty, would undermine social programs, would undermine medicare, would ruin old age assistance. Is he still pursuing those perceptions with respect to the North American free trade agreement? Now after five years have passed that medicare is in place, old age assistance, social programs are in place, does he still persist in viewing the North American free trade agreement as anything but a recitation of the rules under which all three nations will trade in the future? Does he want to continue with the perceptions purveyed by the New Democratic Party that this somehow undermines our social programs, undermines our sovereignty and thus gain support publicly on the basis of that public fraud?

Madam Speaker, the questioner posed a number of issues. Let me attempt to deal with one or two of them.
He quotes John Kenneth Galbraith but neglects to add what Mr. Galbraith on occasion said, and that is that although he advocated the negotiation of a U.S.-Canada free trade agreement he stressed, and stressed repeatedly, the need for a strong Canadian domestic policy to ensure that Canadians benefit from freer trade.
We have seen an absence on the part of this government of an effective and comprehensive adjustment assistance program that would have allowed Canadians to take up such an opportunity. Let me add also that Mr. Galbraith on that occasion spoke of the need for Canada to strengthen in the face of the United States' pervasive influence in our country our own cultural institutions.
What has this government done? Look at its record. It has cut the CBC allocations. It has reduced spending in the film area. It has reduced the support for Canadian writing, for Canadian publishing. It has left ambiguity in its policies on book publishing and now on magazine publishing, a whole range of issues which would have supported a stronger Canadian culture and a stronger Canadian consciousness of ourselves in the face of the freer trade agreement that was being discussed.
I think if the hon. member wants to quote John Kenneth Galbraith he should quote fully from his stance.
As for whether I thought that Canadians should proceed with the free trade agreement, no. We are engaged in some sort of historical review here. I speak for myself, but I believe I speak for my colleagues on this side of the House as well, that the negotiation of the U.S.-Canada free trade agreement was a mistake in two ways.
In broad terms, it enhanced or increased the pervasive influence of one other country in our economy, but more particularly in our society. That I think was a serious mistake. We should have remained freer traders on a global basis, not on a continental basis.
Second, this government failed to provide Canadians, as I said a moment ago, with the adjustment assistance needed to make a reality of the free trade agreement if it was determined to have such an agreement. It failed on that count as well.
The additional way in which this government failed to provide for Canadian interests in the free trade agreement was to look beyond the continent and to emphasize the opportunities for Canadian freer trade in Asia and in Europe matched with an effective program of adjustment assistance.

Madam Speaker, if the member had addressed the question of NAFTA in a serious way, he would have recognized that we in the Official Opposition have for two years called for stronger provisions in the agreement on environmental standards and on labour standards.
Those stronger standards which we called for in 1991 were rejected by the government. The agreement that it negotiated does not contain those broader standards, those stronger standards which we were advocating.
The irony, and it is something of an irony, is that it is the new President of the United States who has come forward with an initiative in that area. He said that he does want to change NAFTA itself but he has proposed two major and possibly three side agreements, certainly one on environment and one on labour standards.
We on our part would welcome a prospect that those side agreements about which we know virtually nothing might be the opportunity to address our concerns in respect of labour and environmental standards. Recognizing that environmental and even labour issues rarely respect national boundaries, the Liberal Party has argued that these issues must be addressed in a multilater-

al North American context. Even without a free trade agreement we should be addressing such questions.
Among other things, we who regard this as a serious debate and not an occasion for a little bit of silly theatre have proposed a trilateral commission for monitoring environmental and labour matters among the three countries with powers to make findings and recommendations. We seek a clearly defined process for developing common standards and then for harmonizing such standards upward. We want to establish an early warning system in environmental and labour disputes, one which would flag such disputes before they escalate into mutually destructive trade wars.
It is for those reasons that we took the initiative two years ago to urge stronger labour standards, stronger environmental standards in the North American free trade agreement and it is for that reason that we continue to pursue that policy and indeed a policy of seeking real substance on a subsidies code and an anti-dumping code as major changes that are needed to the North American free trade agreement.

Madam Speaker, I am honoured to participate in the debate this afternoon on this motion.
What we are talking about here is the stifling of debate and when debate is stifled we talk about a constriction of democracy. It has come down to this constriction of democracy, which is something that everyone in this Chamber should be most concerned about.
This legislation has been before this House of Commons for a grand total of four hours and five minutes. One wonders about the public's response when their elected representatives deal with such a fundamental change in our economic constitution and only give it four hours and five minutes. In fact, the Journals branch of the House of Commons said that the time of the actual debate, that is the time spent talking, was two hours and five minutes. The other two hours got lost in procedural arguments. We had two hours and five minutes to change the economic constitution of our country. We should all be ashamed of ourselves.
Debate does not just occur here in the House of Commons. It occurs out in society generally. It is our responsibility as elected representatives not just to hold forth here but to talk to our constituents and listen to our constituents. The debate ferments throughout society.
The filter through which that debate often occurs is the media. I would like to focus the first portion of my debate on the constriction of democracy on the media because they have a role here which they have not taken seriously. I will give an example.
I was down in Washington six weeks ago with my colleagues from Sault Ste. Marie, Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca and Mission-Coquitlam examining the side deals on the environment and labour and meeting with members of Congress and the U.S. Senate, environmental groups and labour groups. We held a press conference on the afternoon of Tuesday, March 16. Fifty representatives of the media were there. They engaged with us and inquired about what was going on in Canada, how we saw the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement and how we saw the negotiations on the side agreements on the environment and labour.
The next day, after a three-hour stop in Baltimore airport during which my colleague from Esquimalt- Juan de Fuca in better health than he is today played Nerf football with the kids in the airport, we came back to the House of Commons. My colleague from Esquimalt-Juan de Fuca was up on his feet in Question Period with a lead question on the North American free trade agreement. I was the second questioner with a question on the environment. After Question Period, as is usual, we went out to the lobby to engage with the media and not one journalist, not one representative of the media asked us any questions. When we talk about stifling of debate and complicity I think the media also have to take some responsibility.
If this trade deal goes ahead people will say: "Why did you not stop it? Why did you not tell us?" The way we do that as elected representatives is through the filter of the media.
I will give another example. That debate was introduced into the House of Commons on Thursday, March 25, an important day. It was also the day that the Minister of National Defence announced her candidacy for the leadership. I do not think that was an accident, a coincidence. It was a planned tactic to focus the media's attention on the defence minister's candidacy and away from the introduction of the North American free trade agreement into the House of Commons.
Canada's national newspaper, as it likes to call itself, The Globe and Mail, devoted five pages on March 26 to the defence minister but not one page or one word about NAFTA being introduced into the House of Commons. If that is not complicity I do not know what is.
The Tories control the media.

I am not saying that the Tories control the media.
I would now like to turn to the complicity of the Liberals on this issue. When the final vote came on March 31 there were some very interesting absences in the House. This was on the vote on second reading of the North American free trade agreement where the principle of the bill was determined. There were 37 missing Liberals. The member for Vancouver Quadra, the man who said it was the fight of his life in the 1988 election, was somehow otherwise engaged. The vote was 113 in favour to 94 opposed. At that vote 42 out of 44 New

Democrats were there. One was attending his mother's funeral and the other one was in Europe on parliamentary business.
We believe this is a bad deal for Canada. We were willing to be inconvenienced. We were willing to get here. One member flew in from British Columbia, the member for Prince George-Bulkley Valley. He flew in from his riding, got here at 4.30, voted at six o'clock and left at 6.40 to go back to his riding. We did so because we believe that this is a bad deal. We are willing to fight this deal.
The Liberals paired with the government on that legislation. The reason they did that is because they are acting in complicity with the government on this issue. They do not have a policy on the free trade agreement. The reason the Liberals do that is because they want to go along with the Conservative government, the transnational corporations and the media. To give credit, my own paper has done a number of editorials condemning the North American free trade agreement.
There are isolated divergences of views out there. I am not asking the media to agree with my view I am just asking them to fulfil their responsibility in putting it before the Canadian public. I am asking the so-called Official Opposition to get its act together and get a position on this issue.
We are talking about complicity and we are talking about a constriction of democracy. The constriction of democracy is happening now. It certainly will happen if NAFTA is passed because it will inadvertently constrict any future government's ability to act.
The boys are restless in the House today. They do not like it when their game is called but it has been. It is a shame to have only two hours and five minutes of debate in this Chamber on such a fundamental change of Canadian policy.
I hope the Liberals and the government are thoroughly ashamed of themselves.

Madam Speaker, I really do not know what to say. We seem to be interfering in a lovers' quarrel here about who did less in the last election or who did more to get defeated. I hesitate to interfere because it was kind of neat to watch.
We are debating the question of NAFTA and the use of time allocation. I want to put it right on the record that as a former House leader, parliamentary secretary to the House leader and minister of state for the House leader, I never hesitated to use closure to stop what was nothing more than an out and out blatant filibuster. I make no apologies for it and will live with that.
The public recognizes a filibuster and an argument without merit or facts. I am prepared to go to the people and discuss closure with them at any time.
I thought it would be useful in view of the debate which has taken place so far from the other side to add a bit of further substance from this side of the House to this debate.
I am pleased to participate in the debate because it gives me an opportunity to set the record straight. There is no question that since 1984 our government has given a high priority to a reform of Canada's intellectual property laws as a component of our agenda for economic renewal. We have recognized the need for patent laws that protect ideas and innovation and attract investment. We make no apologies for those principles. Attracting investment creates jobs and we all know that.
We have had to fight every step of the way in our effort to modernize and streamline those laws. Over the years the hon. members opposite have tried in vain to halt our progress in this effort.
In the last Parliament they used every obstruction tactic at their disposal in an effort to defeat or delay the first phase of patent reform. During the last Parliament, Bill C-22, an amendment to the Patent Act was given first reading on November 7, 1986. The Liberals and the NDP in the House obstructed the bill to such an extent that it was not forwarded to the other place until May 6, 1987. That was some time allocation, some closure.

Our experience with Bill C-22 served as a warning that we could not afford as a government or a country to see a similar delay in the passage of Bill C-91, the second phase of patent reform. Since 1987 when Bill C-22 was passed, the international community has moved significantly in the direction of stronger patent protection. Canada, the only developed nation in the world with compulsory licensing of medicines was becoming more and more isolated on this issue.
The opposition parties enjoy being isolated on issues. They feel it is sort of a badge of honour to be out of step with the rest of the world and the people. We see it today. We see it in all of their policies.
We were rapidly becoming less attractive for investment in pharmaceuticals than our major trading partners. In December 1991 this growing global consensus was reflected in the intellectual property provisions of the draft text that everyone hoped would resolve the deadlock in the Uruguay round of GATT. It provided a regime for intellectual property protection which made compulsory licensing for pharmaceuticals unacceptable. Following on the GATT, the NAFTA which was signed by Canada, U.S. and Mexico on December 17, 1992 contains the same provisions.
Meeting international trade obligations was one reason for moving forward with this legislation but there are others and I want to take a minute to discuss them. We introduced Bill C-91 because it was in our own best interests as a country and as Canadians.
The pharmaceutical industry is in the process of restructuring globally. It is reorienting its operations to serve global markets more efficiently and to select the most competitive business environment it can find for investment in new facilities. The degree of patent protection provided for innovations is a critical factor. With our former system of compulsory licensing quite frankly we could not attract this kind of investment nor could we have hoped to preserve some 20,000 jobs in this sector. Bill C-91 was a step in the right direction.
However, I must say I found it distressing that many of the arguments voiced from the opposition benches during Bill C-91 were nothing but deja vu and nothing but a rehash of the tired old arguments made in the other place when it tried to thwart the government's legislation in 1987.
Back in 1987 the Liberals maintained that the amendments to the Patent Act would result in higher drug prices. Let me quote Senator Theriault who told the other place that: "By removing the competitive element provided by generic drugs in the industry Bill C-22 will undoubtedly result in huge price increases". That was June 25, 1987 on page 1403 of the Hansard of the other place.
Then we had Senator Bonnell who felt that we were encouraging the research of multinational drug companies at the expense of disadvantaged Canadians who would have to pay higher drug prices. "For goodness' sake", he said from his safe seat in the Senate, "do not take research money off the backs of the sick, the hospitalized, the infirm and the aged by increasing drug prices". That was on August 13, 1987.
In a similar manner Senator Buckwold raised the spectre of fear. That is an age-old Liberal trick. If one wants to talk about patents there is one party that has the patent on raising fear without substance. The NDP I must say-I see their Whip is here-cannot come close to our friends the Liberals in raising the spectre of fear without substance. They own the patent on that. It is not even a 20-year patent. It came with the constitution of the Liberal Party.
What did he say? That is what he said. Senator Buckwold said: "In my opinion if we pass this bill we will be doing a great disservice to the people of Canada. We will be adding to the problem of health costs. We will be denying drugs to people who would otherwise have bought them and who desperately need them". We passed it and I challenge Senator Buckwold to name one.
Me.

Bill C-91 gives the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board tough new powers. These are some of these new powers. It allows the board to better influence introductory prices for new patented drugs. It authorizes the board to order price reductions or penalties which could compensate for past excessive prices and deter excessive pricing practices. It provides for stiff fines and imprisonment for failure to comply with the board's orders and gives the board's orders the same force and effect as an order of the Federal Court.
Again, many of the Liberals both in the House and in the other place had dire predictions such as the drug manufacturers would not double their research and development as a portion of sales as they had promised to do.
Senator Theriault said: "As far as research and development is concerned it is clear. It is not Bill C-22 which will increase its level in Canada. We have nothing but promises and commitments from the pharmaceutical industry which has never proved quite reliable. There is nothing in Bill C-22 which would compel it to meet its commitments".
Senator Bonnell added: "In the original bill there is not five cents guaranteed to go into research. That is just a promise".
We know now that the effect of the changes to the Patent Act was indeed to open the gates. Open the gates to what? It was to a flood of new investment by the pharmaceutical companies and the industry has lived up to its commitments.
In fact the fourth report of the Patented Medicine Prices Review Board points out that the ratio of research and development to sales by the companies that filed patents with the board in 1991 now stands at 9.7 per cent. Total expenditures on research and development for these companies grew to $376.4 million last year. That is an increase of 23 per cent from 1990.
Where were the senators? I hope the senators will read some of these things and go to confession and do what they can to try to redeem themselves for their doubts.
Here is the one I like. Here is a Liberal senator who typifies the confidence that Liberals have in themselves and Canadians. Here is a typical Liberal senator with a typical Liberal line.
During the debates on the old Bill C-22 Senator Buckwold expressed doubts about whether Canada had the capacity to play a major role in the international pharmaceutical industry. This is a typical Liberal inferiority complex. He said: "I do not know how the government can be so naive as to really believe that suddenly Canada will become a major player in the research world". That is a typical lack of confidence in the country and in Canadians that we see everyday from our friends in the Liberal Party.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I apologize if I have offended the rules, although I must say I was surprised. I did not bring this subject to the House today; others did.
I assume they are following the debate very closely wherever they may be.
The minister in his opening comments referred to this motion today. I will quote it because he came out with such an excellent line. He said: "It is a stunning display of hypocrisy". He went on to say that the best way to stifle debate, which is what this motion alleges this government is doing, is to not participate in it.
The New Democratic Party says it is fighting this whole issue, yet does it take advantage of the opportunities that exist to participate in debates on this subject? That, of course, is a good question.
I presume, Mr. Speaker, if I am not allowed to make reference to who may or may not be in the House I am not supposed to say who is or is not in a committee at any given time. I am supposed to be at that committee right now. I would like to be at that committee right now. I
Supply
feel it is pre-eminent for me to be here in my place as parliamentary secretary to the minister to put a few points on the record that are very important. However I notice that after three hours of hearings which that committee held today, the New Democratic Party members who were there have yet to ask a question. That is what we have had in terms of their participation before this committee.
When there is an opportunity to participate in debate one wonders what is really lying behind it. Is it an exercise in the kind of histrionics we have seen from the New Democratic Party? The member for Saanich-Gulf Islands spoke earlier about the fact, and I take what she is saying to be true, that only two hours and five minutes were devoted in this House to actual debate of second reading of Bill C-115.
She neglected to mention that an additional two or three hours of House time were taken up with histrionics. Her distinguished and learned colleagues were banging their desks like a bunch of school children. Another of her colleagues got up and used unparliamentary language, forcing one of the best and most patient Speakers this House has ever seen to throw him out.
Why? Only he can say. I would not want to impute motive because that breaks the rules too. I did notice he made it to TV that night, even though my hon. friend from Saanich-Gulf Islands says "the media have become a Tory conspiracy in this country". Some members may not have heard her say that. I was really quite amazed. I know the Prime Minister will be interested to hear that The Toronto Star is now a Tory rag, as is The Ottawa Citizen, and goodness knows what the CBC has become. Evidently they are all part of the plot to do in the NDP.
I think the NDP members are doing an adequate job of that all by themselves. They do not need our help; they are doing a good job all on their own.
They say we are rushing this whole NAFTA through. I believe the hon. member for Kamloops used the phrase that we were "trying to sneak this trade deal through the House of Commons". Sneak it through in the quiet and the dark of the night no doubt is what he is saying. I do not know, but I wonder why, in view of that, on September 16, 1992 in this very House he said in questioning the Prime Minister: "The Prime Minister will also know that NAFTA as a trade deal is divisive, is

controversial and has major political overtones. We already know that a major government advertising program is under way to promote NAFTA throughout the country".
I recall that day. I was here that day and I am sure all members were here that day when he got up and chastised the government for providing information about NAFTA to all Canadians. He chastised the government for doing that, for propagandising it I suppose is what he meant. That information was put before Canadians so many months ago, but now we are sneaking the deal through the House.
Let us take a look at this business of sneaking the deal through the House. Earlier today the minister in his remarks talked a little bit about the process by which the NAFTA came to be agreed to from a Canadian perspective. He went through a litany of all the process that went on. He made reference to 311 Canadians who had served on the various advisory committees of the government that went into developing Canada's participation in that.
He made reference to over 100 meetings of all those committees representing every manner of organization in Canada that had an interest in trade that the minister talked about in his remarks.
We come to the matter of this bill and the process of discussion by this House of NAFTA. I must find my piece of paper because I do not want to mislead the House with inaccurate information.
As I mentioned in a question earlier last spring the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade held hearings on the subject of North American free trade, before a deal was reached, so that Canadians could make known their views on the subject. They held 27 public meetings, heard from 203 witnesses and in addition received another 95 submissions.
After the deal was signed and agreed to in August, it was made public to the Canadian people at the beginning of November and a subcommittee of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade had hearings. It held 28 public meetings, heard from 124 groups, 203 witnesses, received 95 submissions, 23 exhibits and held hearings in 9 Canadian cities.
We snuck it from coast to coast. We snuck it right through the country. That was hearings on the substance of the agreement itself.
In addition, I might say that NAFTA is not a subject that has failed to make its way into Hansard. As a matter of fact it has been raised on at least 237 different sitting days in this Parliament. Three hundred and four questions not including supplementaries have been asked on the subject of NAFTA and the bill has been debated on the floor of this House. There have been 22 members' statements, 14 positions and five full opposition days devoted to this subject, today being one of them.
Today the subject of debate is not the substance of NAFTA. It is not even the substance of Bill C-115. If my hon. friends in the NDP think there was not enough time debating in this House on Bill C-115, why did they introduce today, when we had several hours available, a frivolous topic on this process of discussion? Why are we today not debating the substance if that is what is needed before this House?
They only can that question because I certainly cannot. That is something I really do not know. All I can say is it seems to me there are two messages that the Canadian people are passing to the members of this House. One of them came out loud and clear in the Spicer report.
What Canadians want to see of their parliamentarians if they turn on the parliamentary channel is substance. They want to see bona fide debate. They want to see intelligent discourse, bringing out different sides of issues.
They are not interested in people trying to get on television by ripping up documents and littering the floor of the Commons or by people entertaining in discussions of parliamentary procedure to get themselves thrown out so that all the TV cameras will rush to them. They want to see Canadians acting in a responsible serious manner, debating serious issues on the floor of this place. That is one message that is coming out loud and clear.
The other message that I am getting from Canadians all the time is why do you fool around so much? Why do you not get on with it? Why do you not get things done?
It is interesting to recall that on the floor of the British House of Commons the Maastricht treaty at second reading was debated for five hours. That was it and the
May 5, 1993

Maastricht treaty was thereby approved by the House of Commons in England.
There are those who would have this House debate endlessly, forever and ever and never come to an agreement whatsoever. Then of course the government would be criticized for never getting anything done. It is great if you are in the opposition. Either way have it.
If they go, get on with it and do it, you criticize them for bulldozing. If they do not do it, or you are able to delay the process so that nothing gets done then you criticize them for not doing anything.
It is like watching the budget come down last week. What do we hear from the finance critic of the Liberal Party? Where is the deficit? You did not do a thing. There is nothing there. Then all these colleagues get up and complain because we cut here and we cut here and we cut here. Which way is it? Which side of the fence are they sitting on today? That is a question that sometimes one might wish to put.
We have also heard this. Why are you doing this legislation now? The Americans have not passed it through their Congress. The Mexicans have not passed it through their Congress. Why are we rushing ahead to do this? I will tell you, Mr. Speaker, that this government does not take its legislative directives from south of the border. This government brings forward legislation, enters into international agreements that it deems to be in the interests of Canadians that are going to contribute to job creation in Canada, that are going to contribute to economic growth for the benefit of Canadians. That is what motivates and drives this government.
One of my NDP colleagues today was bragging how she went to Washington and heard what everybody thinks in Washington. Guess what? We on this side of the House are more interested in what Canadians think. That is one of the reasons, for example, that we did not see any point in having Canadian parliamentary committees do what the New Democratic Party wanted and that is to send, at great cost to the Canadian taxpayer, a bunch of Canadian members of Parliament touring all over the United States and Mexico to hear what Mexicans and Americans think of this trade deal. That is not
