what we think our role is. Our role is to respond to what is in the interest of Canada.
The hon. member for Etobicoke North in his remarks said: "Well, the deal is dead anyway, the Americans say that themselves". Quite simply that is not true.
We had an interesting time last week when a U.S. official, a high official of the American government, Mr. Panetta, the Director of Office Management and Budget Director and Representative, U.S. Administration, was quoted as saying that the trade deal would not pass Congress now. He used the word dead. He said it would be dead if it went up to Congress now. That is very true, I guess. I do not know but it is interesting. That was about a week ago and everybody jumped on Mr. Panetta and said that this is not the case at all. The President, for example, made the comment: "Panetta just got discouraged over battles ahead". Rather than being angry Mr. Clinton said:"I need him to get his spirits up. He just had a bad day yesterday. He got his spirits down. I want to back him up. I do not want to take him out to the woodshed".
I wonder if my hon. friend from Etobicoke North knows that on April 28, 12 Republican senators wrote a letter to the President of the United States indicating that they were going to support him all the way on this legislation. The letter is right here and if any members would like a copy I would be glad to provide it. I think the important point to bear in mind on that is NAFTA is not going right now to the U.S. Congress. NAFTA will go to the U.S. Congress in four or five months.
I recall in 1988, for example, that if there had been an election held in June 1988, this government was at 22 per cent in the polls. They would have probably been as dead as ducks too except the election was not held then. It was held four or five months later. It was held on November 21, 1988, and what happened on that day? A resounding majority re-elected this government once again because the Canadian people were not fooled by the shenanigans and the scaremongering of people on the other side. I am saying that really we have to set our own agenda and we have to follow through on that agenda.
I want to say a word or two about this committee. When the House leader for the New Democratic Party spoke he said that we put closure into this committee on the very first day. If my hon. friends from the NDP do not understand it, I think it is important that Canadians

May 5, 1993
Supply
understand the role and function of a legislative committee. The process of legislation, a bill, a proposed law is introduced for first reading and tabled in the House. Then it comes back to this place where the principle of it is debated on second reading. The House either approves of that principle or the House does not. If the House approves of that principle then the bill goes to a legislative committee for legislative study. In other words the task and the role of that committee is to study that legislation and see if the enactment of that legislation will achieve the goals and objectives set down by the government in the official speech that the government makes in introducing second reading debate. That is what a legislative committee does. Then of course the bill comes back to the House where it may be amended at report stage and it is debated finally at third reading.
The purpose of the legislative committee studying Bill C-115 is not to travel around Canada and ask what people think about NAFTA because that is not the function of a legislative committee. The function of a legislative committee is to study this legislation and see if it does what it is supposed to do. In this case its purpose is fairly simple. It is supposed to take that NAFTA deal, the big thick book that was ripped up by the House leader of the NDP today, and effect it as law. That is what is the role of our committee. Our committee has brought before it about 40 different experts who have assisted the committee in doing that.
I put the motion before the committee to plan out the committee's work in an orderly fashion. The New Democratic Party made it clear that it was not interested in the substance of the exercise. It was simply interested in trying to get as much publicity out of fighting the NAFTA as it could. It really did not care whether we got down to doing what the committee was there to do or not. That has certainly shown in the way the committee has conducted itself.
The contribution of NDP members in that committee has been somewhere between nil and extremely minimal. There have been days when they did not ask a single question.
I must say my hon. friends from the Liberal Party have attempted to participate in a very effective way, my hon. friend from Cape Breton Highlands-Canso in particular. However the most effective members of that committee, if I do say so myself, have been the Progressive Conservative members who did their homework, studied the legislation and questioned those witnesses. Anybody who doubts what I say need only examine the transcripts which are available for all to see.
No, that is not what the NDP wanted. What the members of the NDP wanted was another road show. This time they not only wanted it across Canada, but in Mexico, the United States and who knows where else. Now that they have heard that Chile and Venezuela are interested in joining as well maybe they would want the committee to go down to Chile and Venezuela and check out those countries also. I am afraid that is not the role and function of the legislative committee.
I will conclude with this last point. Closure and time allocation are instruments passed by a Liberal government. They were brought in, as they would be, by a government. Let us be frank, an opposition would never bring in a time allocation rule. They were brought in so that if there was no co-operation among the parties, they would give the government the opportunity to do what the people elected it to do and that specifically is to run the country and to carry on its responsibilities. That is their purpose.
Under 78(1) of the rules there is consultation which has gone on. Even under section 78(2), even if only one party will agree there could be time allocation. But if what you are getting back is what this government has got back time and time again, not just on Bill C-115 but on Bill C-91 and on several other pieces of legislation, no co-operation, then time allocation is there to be used.
In closing, it is interesting to note that from 1980 to 1984 this procedure was used on 18 bills by the Liberal government. Between 1984 and 1988 it was used on 16 bills by this government. Between 1988 and 1992 it was used on 21 bills. The practice is pretty standard on both sides of the House.

Mr. Speaker, your comments here are giving us the possibility to ask some questions.
We talk about NAFTA but we should also have been talking about the free trade agreement with the United States. We have to ask ourselves what it brought to Canada. Was it a positive or a negative? In my opinion it was negative because with the free trade agreement with the United States we lost about 450,000 jobs mostly in manufacturing. Therefore it was a bad deal.
To point out that it was a bad deal, our current account deficit is $30 billion. We go deeper into debt every year. This money we owe to foreign countries.
Look at this tremendous number: $30 billion. That is the current account deficit. This happened with the free trade agreement with the United States. We are losing money and we are not benefiting. Before the free trade agreement it was about $9 billion. Now it is $30 billion a year.
As far as our trade with Mexico is concerned, Mexico exports $1.7 billion to Canada and we export $0.6 billion to Mexico. The question is this: Does the hon. member believe that if we have an agreement with Mexico to have more manufacturing jobs in Canada that we are going to export more to Mexico than Mexico is going to export to us? This is the question. Can the member prove it?

That is a 19.2 per cent increase. Canada's merchandise trade surplus with the United States was $17.7 billion, which is a 27.3 per cent increase over 1991.

speakerposition: Bloc Québécois Caucus Chair
speechtext:
I would have a few comments to make, Mr. Speaker. In 1988, when I ran as a Conservative, my main purpose was to support free trade. I worked very hard and made at least 75 speeches to tell people that I was for free trade. I still agree with free trade, because I sincerely believe in it, especially for the Montreal region. For example, we know that the Montreal market is within 800 kilometres of 75 million consumers with whom we can do business. It is much more profitable for us in Montreal to do business with Boston, New York, Buffalo and Toronto than with Vancouver. Not that we have anything against Vancouver, but we realized that it is more profitable for the Montreal area to do business north-south.
Basically, the big problem is what came later; after concluding the free trade agreement in December 1988, the government some seven or eight months later let interest rates climb at the same time as the dollar rose. This was very harmful to our small businesses which wanted to export to the United States. That is the real problem. Free trade is not the issue but rather the government's handling of it which prevented free trade from succeeding.
I want to ask the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade a question which concerns Quebec in particular. When will his government finally decide to leave all manpower training to Quebec, so that Quebec can properly train the workers needed for our small and medium-sized businesses to be more productive? That is also a major problem we have in

Quebec. We cannot assert our responsibilities because the government still stubbornly insists on keeping jurisdiction over labour force training, knowing veiy well that Quebec is responsible for this field because we already have the institutions in place. All we lack is the money needed to do so properly because the federal government collects taxes but does not return the funds required for manpower training. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, briefly I want to say to my hon. friend that the facts are there as to the success of the FTA.
The facts are also there as to the success of this government in bringing inflation under control for the first time in 30 years in this country. These are the factors that are going to contribute not only to the rest of Canada but indeed to Quebec.
As to his specific question about manpower training, I must say that I am not sure exactly what that has to do with the motion on the floor today. I am sure that if he would like to put that in a question to the Minister of Employment and Immigration some day in the House he will get a more thorough answer than I can properly provide at this time.

Mr. Speaker, the debate we are having here today is not just about the process. It is also about trust.
It is very difficult to have any trust in this government's economic agenda when we have seen case after case where it is just not working. I want to bring this down to a concrete example.
Tomorrow in my city we are having a burial for one of the most productive and profitable assembly plants. It is the GM van plant in Scarborough, Ontario. This is a company that has made close to $2.2 billion in the last 10 years and these are General Motors numbers.
The 3,500 skilled men and women who are losing their jobs see a situation where General Motors just in the last 18 months went from hiring 6,000 people to 60,000 people in Mexico. Put this NAFTA agreement in the context of the first assembly plant to be shut down in Canadian history that has been making money. We are not talking about a loser here. We are talking about a cash cow for General Motors. We see what is going on in Mexico and this really presents a problem for people.
I believe that one of the real difficulties here is the issue of trust in the government's economic agenda and platform. I would ask the member this: If a General Motors assembly plant in his riding shut down affecting 3,500 direct jobs and another 8,000 to 10,000 indirect jobs how does he approach his constituents? How does he say: "Hey, NAFTA is great because General Motors is hiring an extra 40,000 to 50,000 people in Mexico and we are losing a plant to Flint, Michigan"? How does he sell that kind of thing?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade

Mr. Speaker, NAFTA is not even in place yet and he is blaming this closure on NAFTA already. That is really kind of bizarre. I would say to my hon. friend that I do not have any General Motors plants in my riding but I do have a Michelin tire plant. Before the FTA it employed about 1,400 people. Today, notwithstanding the world recession that is the biggest crippling factor in terms of plant closures, not only in this country but throughout the. western world, that Michelin tire plant is employing 200 people more than it did when the FTA was brought in.
I would invite my hon. friend to look at statistics just released by the International Monetary Fund predicting that Canada will lead the G-7 nations in growth in employment and in growth in real GDP in 1993 and 1994. That is the result of this government.

What if the Michelin plant went to Mexico?

Mr. Speaker, I want to make sure that the people watching us know what we are talking about. As you know, the government has taken certain liberties, and I will quote the motion before the House today: "That this House condemns the stifling of debate through the misuse of closure by the enforcement of time allocation on NAFTA and other important trade-related legislation". There are three points I would like to raise in this connection.

The three points are as follows. I want to talk about the closure and time limitation because I think it is important for Canadians to know how it is being used and how frequently it has been used. I want to talk about my party's position on NAFTA and the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement and I want to talk about other positions, namely those of the NDP and the national party.

My first point is this: Why limit debate on what is probably one of the most important if not the most important question for Canadians in this country today? Why? I really do not understand. The government knows this bill scares Canadians. Why? Because with all the statistics and all the information the negotiators put on the table, and the different positions being taken on the matter, Canadians realize that today, in 1993, the chances of keeping one's job are not as good as they were in the past. We see men and women who are motivated, well educated and know how to handle themselves but cannot find a job, and they believe this is largely due to the government's policies. Of course there is also the recession, but it is also, at least partly, due to the free trade agreement with the United States.
People are afraid this government is more concerned about getting re-elected than about the interests of Canada's workers. Mr. Speaker, you are well aware of this, and so are my colleagues on the government side. This scares Canadians, who think: If I do not have a job-and it seems my chances of finding one are not very good-or if I do have a job which I could lose, will I not

be sacrificed because this government's first priority is to be re-elected?
Consider the budget, where we see the same approach. In this budget the party comes first. People are afraid that NAFTA is more important than Canadians and that the government's main concern is to be reelected. If this was the first time people might be patient. However this procedure to limit debate on legislation has been used nearly 40 times in four years. My first example goes back to 1988 during the debate on free trade and other bills, including unemployment insurance. The government did the same thing to the debate on the GST, a tax cordially detested by all Canadians, and then unemployment insurance again and a second time during the GST debate. These are only a few examples.
I am glad I have these notes: three pages on Bill C-81, the referendum bill, and there is more. The government imposed closure on NAFTA. This is the second time. And remember Bill C-93, Mr. Speaker, when the government was beaten because it did not do its homework. It claimed it would save money and increase government efficiency. When we asked for proof, it did not have any. What did it do? It decided it was better to stop the debate because they were being crushed and humiliated, and that is the kind of attitude that scares Canadians.
Last week, the budget was brought down. I think a budget should at least provide some hope for a country that is suffering. Canadians are suffering today, not me, not necessarily my colleagues, but many Canadians. I asked the following question: What hope is there in the budget for men and women who are unemployed? More than 1.6 million Canadians are unemployed, and some people say it is twice that many. What hope is there in this budget for the 2.7 million people who are on welfare? I also asked the following question: What hope is there for the 2.2 million men, women and children who will be fed by food banks in Canada this year? The same questions could be asked about this bill: What hope is there for the unemployed, for people on welfare, for the men, women and children who will be fed by food banks this year in Canada?
Some people say: Yes, but we have to stop talking, we have to stop the debate on this bill. We have to go ahead. I say: Sure, I agree, but let the members have a

reasonable amount of time to express their views. For instance, there are a number of questions that should have been asked: Will this bill have a negative impact on Canada's sovereignty? If this bill is passed, will it have a negative impact on culture in Canada? And we could ask many more questions that are very important to Canadians.
I referred to the use of this procedure to limit debate. And I said that this procedure had been used far too often, nearly 40 times in four years, on bills that were very important to Canadians, and I think that is very unfortunate.
I also said, and I want to get back to this, that there were still questions to be asked and answers outstanding.
There is another point that has always bothered me, a point I raised when the bill on free trade with the United States was tabled. The government knows perfectly well which industries will be affected by this agreement, if it is signed. And since the government knows which sectors will be affected, they should tell us. And then we have to tell them: Listen, what kind of training and retraining programs do you have to help the men and women who will be displaced? You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that during the last debate on the subject, the Prime Minister of Canada said we would have the best possible training and retraining programs to protect the men and women displaced by job losses. We are still waiting for these programs. What industries will be affected? What programs will be put in place to meet the needs of these people, these displaced workers? These are basic, very important questions.
Now some people ask me what our position would be if we were in power. Our policy is veiy clear. Mr. Speaker, you surely know that in the last election campaign, we came out very strongly against this bill. Five years have passed since the last election and the situation must be reviewed. We have said that we must be absolutely sure that agreed-upon regulations apply to both countries and that an arbitration tribunal will judge cases of conflict fairly. Moreover, we should ensure our sovereignty over water and energy. We should also ensure protection of the environment and of workers' rights. That is what we said. We said that if we could not obtain
these agreements, as U.S. President Clinton is now calling for as well, the deal should be cancelled.
Now some ask what the position of the left and of the National Party is. I asked them, if they were in power, would they think an agreement should be negotiated with the United States. They answered yes. Then I asked what they would negotiate. I told them to show us black on white what they would negotiate, because it is very important for Canadians to know exactly what a political party would do in this kind of negotiation with another country. I also asked them to tell me what they intended to accomplish, as well as what they intended to negotiate. Give me evidence that you can achieve such objectives. Unfortunately, I have not had any answer so far.

Let me say that the members of the Liberal Party of Canada recognize that Canada is a trading nation. We are committed to open and fair trade. We recognize that roughly one in five jobs is directly dependent upon exports. We want to secure an increased access to world markets. We believe it is dangerous to be too dependent upon one country.
We believe as well, and I can appreciate there is some difference of opinion on this, that the current government has not done as well as it should have in the first trading agreement, nor will it do as well as it should with the second agreement. The first one is the Canada-U.S. trade agreement and the second one is NAFTA.
We find it unfortunate that the NDP national party refuses to accept the global reality and, I am not trying to be unkind, builds protectionist walls around Canada because that is no longer reality today.
We deplore the fact that in 1988 we did not get secure access to the United States market. For example, there were the pork, steel and softwood lumber cases because there were no subsidies or anti-dumping codes. We do not believe we achieved a level playing-field. We believe we need to address that question.
There are a number of government members including the Prime Minister and the Minister for International Trade who are trying to suggest that NAFTA is a fait accompli and is not going to change. That is not what we are hearing. It is far from being carved in stone and my
May 5, 1993

friend and colleague, the minister knows that. It is still open to change if we want to change.
The President of the United States has said he will not accept the accord in its current form and I bet he does not. Since he has indicated that he will not sign it in its present form because he wants some changes to environmental and labour standards, why would we not be seeking that as well?
He has also indicated that he is considering pulling it off the fast track, which would delay the ratification of this agreement. Why are we in a hurry? Why do we not have time to discuss this? This should give us time to re-evaluate our position, particularly-and I do not say this in a partisan way-because this is an election year. Contrary to what my friends from the government side think, there could be a significant change in government and I believe there will be.
Why rush through this? This should be an opportunity to be seized to seek changes to the agreement that are essential to our vital interests. Why does this government intend to sign this off? It seems to me that if it signs it off too quickly it will be surrendering Canada's bargaining position.
We have urged this government to use NAFTA to protect Canadian interests and correct the major shortcomings of the Canada-U.S. trade agreement. My colleague knows that because he is smiling. Whenever he smiles it is an acknowledgement that I am right. When the smile becomes a laugh it is an enthusiastic endorsement of what I have just said.
After eight years and two sets of negotiations that member's government-and he is one of the finer members-has been unable to achieve the principal objective of this trade policy and that is to ensure secure access to the United States market. He knows that. He knows that NAFTA does not provide a common subsidy or anti-dumping code. It does not create binding dispute panels for a quicker settlement process. It does not include environmental and labour standards of any consequence. To add insult to injury, the Tories have been unwilling to put in place a major work force adjustment package after negotiating such a deal.

That is scandalous because the last time the Prime Minister of Canada indicated, with some support from some of his ministers, that we would have the finest training programs in place. The aims of the NAFTA as now spelled out by Clinton and others have shifted in the direction more in keeping with the needs of Canadians and the needs and positions advocated by the Liberal Party.
The Conservatives must not go forward and close this deal. In its current form NAFTA is not the best deal for Canada. Canadians simply cannot afford to have another deal that will take away more jobs, particularly in a period when the economy is really quite precarious.

If it were only a matter of reducing tariff barriers there would be no difficulty and there would be no problem with it.

Water.

The member over here says: "Water" and he is absolutely right. It is a very critical concern that I might add is being listened to very closely in some circles within our neighbour to the south.
Right now as we debate this legislation and whether or not water is actually included in it, there is a proposal just north of my riding, in the riding of my hon. friend from Kamloops, by Canadian and U.S. interests to divert a major portion of the flow of the North Thompson River, move it by pipeline into the storage reservoir for Mica Dam and then through the Columbia River system, to be piped off from the Columbia River by pipeline into the California market. At a recent conference last month in California the U.S. interests were looking at the proposal of Multinational Water and Power on this North Thompson diversion as a test case for the export of water under free trade. That was admitted just last month. We can see they are watching very closely with respect to the control of Canadian resources and how the North American trade agreement and the free trade agreement, for that matter, affect that control.
The government has boasted that Canada's federal water policy prohibits large scale diversions of fresh water. The federal water policy document was drawn up in about 1986-87. It is not a bad document. It has some good policy directions. It is a policy initiative. That is all it is. There is no legislation to back it up. It remains a philosophical document. It is absolutely toothless in terms of any legislative clout.
There was a bill before the House of Commons in the spring of 1988 dealing with the question of water exports which died on the Order Paper. The government has never seen fit to bring back that legislation. There is no legislation protecting Canadian water resources from the possibility of export contracts, inter-basin transfers, diversion by pipeline or tanker export of water.
The government has also suggested the federal water policy would protect Canadian water resources from a challenge under the FTA or under the proposed NAFTA. We heard just a few hours ago one of the senior bureaucrats in government, the deputy assistant attorney general, essentially concede at committee the fact that even if we had strong domestic legislation protecting Canadian water resources, because we did not put a specific provision excluding water in the North American free trade agreement, in any conflicts between this international agreement, this trilateral agreement, the NAFTA, and domestic legislation, the trilateral agreement would take precedence. What does it mean? It does not mean diddley squat whether we have any strong legislation protecting water resources. It does not matter what our federal water policy says. If it was argued under the provisions of the North American trade agreement, and I submit that argument will take place some day, that water is recognized as a commodity or a good of trade under the auspices of the NAFTA and there was a challenge based on that, it would not matter whether we had this legislation. The NAFTA provisions would overrule the federal water policy or any implementing legislation.
There is only one way to get around it and that would be to have the exclusion for water as a commodity or a good of trade actually written into the legislation itself. And it ain't there, Mr. Speaker. We want to know why it is not there.
When we look at certain clauses of the NAFTA bill, we find there is a specific exclusion for raw logs. The government was not totally asleep at the switch, it got an exclusion for raw logs. When it comes to the trade of raw logs, no. It is written into the NAFTA agreement that Canada will not negotiate trade with respect to the export of raw logs.
We also looked at the export of unprocessed fish. It is in the agreement. The government thankfully had the foresight to say that when it comes to unprocessed fish from the Atlantic or from Quebec and the maritimes that it will not be an item of trade. Somehow the government forgot that we have a west coast salmon fishery that has really been taking a beating, but at least it protected Quebec and the maritimes.
However, those two exclusions are in the North American trade agreement, written in black and white. They will take precedence and there is no way that they can overrule on those two situations.
However, there is nothing on water. When it comes to the possibility of water exports, the North American trade agreement is absolutely silent.
The government says: "Our federal water policy does not allow large scale water exports or water diversions". I want to say that Dr. Frank Quinn, who is one of the senior policy advisors in the federal Inland Waters Directorate, has admitted that the government is now reconsidering its position on water exports. That did not come from me, it came from one of the senior bureaucrats.

It means that if the agreement actually provides for the possible export of Canadian waters as a commodity of trade, then any domestic policy or any domestic legislation could be overruled.

He said: Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to stand in this House this evening to debate my private member's motion, M-580. This motion, although deemed not
May 5, 1993

votable by the house management subcommittee, recommends that the government should consider the advisability of amending the Voluntary Firemen's tax exemption from $500 to $1,000 in order to make it more meaningful in the context of inflation and their service to their community.
There is no question in anyone's mind with respect to the exceptional work done by volunteer fire-fighters all across this country. My motion attempts to recognize and pay tribute to these fire-fighters, to pay tribute to their dedication and their selflessness to their communities.
Volunteer fire-fighters serve their communities with very little compensation. Generally, they are given honorariums that cover out of pocket expenses while in the attendance of emergencies, fires or training sessions.
I am confident that no one in this House will disagree that such remuneration is worth every penny that this government now gives.
Section 6(l)(b)(viii) of the Income Tax Act exempts the first $500 of allowances received by these volunteer fire-fighters from taxation. That amount was increased from $300 to $500 for the 1980 taxation year and has remained unchanged. In 1980 very few volunteer firefighters exceeded $500 through a combination of honorariums and fire-call payments.
With annual inflationary increases in those rates the majority of these volunteers are now seeing a portion of that payment subject to tax. The Government of Canada is taking taxes away from these volunteer fire-fighters who are giving up their own time and their own efforts for their communities. For this reason, I believe that this government and this country should be proud to increase that exemption from $500 to $1,000.
Volunteer fire-fighters provide an invaluable and vital service to our communities all across this country. I believe that those men and women who volunteer their services to fight fires in communities across Canada should be exempt from paying taxes on all their fire department disbursements.
Allow me to mention some of the reasons that I hope members on all sides of this House will agree with this motion. First, volunteer fire-fighters are the backbone of the protection of a significant number of communities across this country, not only in rural areas but also in some urban centres across Canada. The majority are

well-trained in fire-fighting, rescue work, first aid, CPR and emergency operations. They are the ones who are called when there is a difficult situation that no one in the community knows how to handle.
These volunteers spend many hours in training, upkeep of their fire stations, care and maintenance of the fire apparatus and the equipment without any remuneration. They drive their privately owned vehicles in response to emergency alarms. Their privately owned vehicles are also used to travel many miles to attend training courses, fire conferences, and fire association meetings, which are all very important in the management of our local fire departments.
Volunteer fire departments are the only service organizations in a number of communities across this country. They are the ones that are out there helping young children in distress. They are the ones that are out there raising money for community arenas and community centres. They are the ones in many small towns across Canada that do the backbone of the work which keeps these small communities together and working together.
The men and women assist in charitable work. They organize and operate minor hockey and baseball teams. In some instances a volunteer fire-fighter is docked his regular pay while he is out on a fire call.
Finally in many volunteer fire departments the moneys received by the members are pooled in a fund and this fund is used to keep up the fire station, buy or construct equipment and apparatus and buy uniforms. Basically they are paying for the community with the service that they provide.
Obviously these men are dedicated volunteers and take great pride in serving their communities. I believe that we must recognize their service and contributions to not only their communities but to Canada.
More important, we as members of Parliament should encourage the spirit of volunteerism in this country. The selfless service of volunteer fire-fighters goes beyond volunteerism because these men and women provide a vital service to our communities.
In my riding of Haldimand-Norfolk there are 13 fire departments all of which support one another and I as their member of Parliament feel they do a very superb job.

Private Members' Business
I can recall how I really grasped the importance of our volunteer fire department. It was during a very tragic fire in my riding and I think you remember that, Mr. Speaker. We had a very large tire fire in my riding and it was then that I saw the men and women of our volunteer fire departments really come together and show the whole world how we in small town Ontario could deal with a situation that nobody thought could be dealt with.
The fire burned for 17 days and if it was not for these men and women who came together I believe that fire would still be burning today.
They left their jobs, homes, farms and their families to fight this fire and we all can be proud of them for doing this. I think we all realize and appreciate the dedicated teamwork and the selfless work that these men and women did on behalf of their communities in Haldi-mand-Norfolk. I think we all as a country and as a community in Haldimand-Norfolk really owe them our gratitude and respect.
To be prepared to be a fire-fighter and to do the job takes time. For example, in the Port Dover fire department in my riding volunteer fire-fighters meet every Thursday evening. They check out the equipment, do the maintenance work, do the vehicle upgrade and they upgrade their skills. Within the region of Haldimand- Norfolk once a month the department does a hose demonstration and hosts a demonstration and instruction session.
Up to five men from each department can take part in these sessions. They are continually going out and upgrading their skills because we know, in the fire department as in everything else, technology is coming fast and they have to know the new techniques and the new ways of fighting fires. The goal in these sessions is to get each volunteer trained in every aspect of the job. These are professionals and we are talking about professionals who take this job very seriously.
Volunteer fire-fighters have made it possible to provide a service to a great many urban and rural communities and municipalities that could not have otherwise afforded to pay a force. We save millions and millions of dollars across this country on a daily basis because of our volunteer fire-fighters.
There are presently 76,290 volunteer fire-fighters across this country. I hope everyone of them knows that we in this House appreciate the hard work and the dedication they give to their communities.
I have been asked to comment on how much this would cost Canadian taxpayers because it is important and I think Canadian taxpayers need to know. When this came out in 1980 and when it was $500 we found that hardly any volunteer fire-fighter used the whole $500 so it would be hard to estimate exactly what this cost would be.
However, at the maximum, if every volunteer firefighter across this country used the extra $500 it would cost approximately $38 million. There is no way in this country that every volunteer fire-fighter would use that but obviously there would be a significant amount of that used.
That is the figure that they throw out. I for one believe that that is a figure that would be well spent in making sure that this country knows, even in these hard economic times, who is providing the services that are saving us money. I think it is a good way to tell Canadians that we appreciate their work and what they are doing for this country.
"The government has argued that increasing the tax exemption would shift the tax burden from one group of Canadians to another." This is from a letter that the Minister of Finance sent to me. He suggested that somehow other Canadians would have to pay for these Canadians getting this tax exemption.
What he did not say and what he forgot to say was that right now these fire-fighters are taking the cost out of providing a service to the rest of the country. The government's attitude is that these fire-fighters are lucky to be getting any kind of tax exemption at all.
In June 1989 I wrote to the minister and outlined the invaluable, selfless service these people provide. I said that these men and women are all doing us a favour. The minister's reply was unfortunate. He said there will be no tax exemption increase.
This is why I brought this motion forward today. I did it to bring attention to this motion again. I know hon. members on all sides of this House have brought this up
May 5, 1993

before. It took me four years to get it drawn out of the opposition motions. Therefore we know how hard it is to put forward something on the floor of the House but I thought it important enough to do this.
I want to conclude. These volunteers are donating their time and they are often risking their lives on behalf of others. They selflessly and non-grudgingly fight fires and all in the name of duty. Surely we owe them more than just thanks. We owe them, I believe, a tax exemption of $1,000 for the next taxation year.
In fact, the sum should be increased periodically to keep up with inflation. This is the least that the Government of Canada can do to recognize the great contribution that these volunteers make to the country. It would offer some incentive, a small incentive, to get more volunteers, fire-fighters.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter L. McCreath (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for International TYade):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for International Trade
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just briefly want to add my voice to the sentiments intended in the motion of my hon. friend. That is, of course, to recognize the selfless and valuable contribution made to communities from coast to coast in this country by voluntary fire departments.
In my South Shore constituency we have about 40 voluntary fire departments and I estimate close to 1,000 voluntary firemen. I would add on top of that, and I know my hon. friend from Haldimand-Norfolk would do the same in his own area, that there are the auxiliaries. They do tremendous work fund raising for the fire departments and contribute in a very significant financial way.
I think it is very important that our communities recognize that. I know in our province of Nova Scotia one of the things the province has done is to provide a special licence plate for automobiles that firemen can put on their cars if they wish. They wear those as a badge of honour and they are pleased to have them.
In Canada for the last 20 years or so we have had the fire service exemplary service medal which recognizes 20 years of voluntary service by fire-fighters. We as members of Parliament sometimes have the opportunity to present those. It is a very happy occasion for us to go to those non-political events and have an opportunity to be with people in the community while they are having a kind of annual celebration of fellowship and good times.
Private Members' Business
As to the specific proposal of my hon. friend, in principle it is hard not to agree with it. These people give so much to the community that we could turn around and say: "Why not have the community recognize that contribution by letting them write off against their income tax an additional amount beyond that $500". Obviously, as a financial measure, it is something that would have to be studied by the government. I appreciate the fact that he gave kind of a ball-park figure as to the cost of that, but I think it is important to know that it is from a budgetary point of view a very costly thing. That is something that would have to be looked at perhaps very well, as he says.
As far as I am concerned it is well worth it to me to know that I am a little bit more secure in my community.
I remember when my mother-in-law's house caught on fire four or five years ago. It was the voluntary fire department that came and saved her house. There was serious damage. In fact Chief Harold Richardson who directed the fire-fighters is retiring this Saturday in Hubbards after many years as chief of that department and after giving a valuable service.
However, that financial implication is there. He indicated that not all firemen take advantage of the existing deduction. Perhaps to them it is because it is a voluntary community service and if there is some form of compensation by way of a tax benefit then maybe a number of them would feel it is not there.
I think this is the important point. It is important that my hon. friend brought this forward. This House and this place should recognize the tremendous contribution made to Canada by voluntary firemen and I join him in saluting those individuals.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I will have the following speakers: the hon. member for The Battle-fords-Meadow Lake next and then I will have the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond, the hon. member for Ontario and the hon. member for Dartmouth in that order.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank you for recognizing me this evening on this important private member's initiative from the hon. member for Haldimand-Norfolk. He is a member with whom I have served on a number of

May 5, 1993
Private Members' Business
delegations and whom I have considerable respect for in this House.
I want to congratulate the member for Haldimand- Norfolk for bringing forward this initiative for us to discuss today. I also want to thank him for, as he put it, sticking with it through the draw process. Having had this idea for over four years here and being able to stick with it through the process of private member's draw is admirable. I very much appreciate the fact that he did it because he should be successful.
This is the type of motion that all members of this House should find extremely easy to support. In fact many members of this House should be trying to do exactly the same thing that the hon. member for Haldimand-Norfolk is attempting to do because many of us have volunteer fire-fighters in our communities all of whom are doing exactly what the hon. member said in his introductory remarks in serving their communities.
I want to tell the member and other members in the Chamber that in supporting today I do so for many of the reasons that have already been outlined, but also because I do support even extending some of the benefit of this tax exemption to other members of emergency response teams in our rural communities who are serving almost on a volunteer basis. They are people like the first-response personnel who quite often attend to accident victims on the highway after vehicle accidents prior to the the ambulances or the doctor arriving; people who volunteer with the ambulance corps from time to time; some of the nurse practitioners in the rural communities. Their service essentially is on a call or need basis and their training allows them to make life in a rural community much more enjoyable because we know that those people are present.
As the hon. member who initiated this motion today indicated, the premise has already been accepted, the exemption exists. In fact the exemption has been increased once in recognition of the costs associated with this as being worthwhile to the community and to our nation. At one point the exemption was $300. For the 1980 tax year. It was increased to $500. Obviously we are now 13 years going into the 14th year since that increase in exemption was allowed.
Government members, particularly those with their hands on the purse-strings, should be looking very seriously at updating and upgrading this important initiative from those 1980 levels to 1993 levels. These people do provide a valuable and vital service to our communities. They are prepared at all hours of the day or night to respond. They are among the most dedicated of the volunteers in our communities.
In rural Canada, we have a very strong volunteer base that improves the quality of life throughout those rural communities. Many of these people who are fire-fighters are dedicating themselves constantly to be ready and available to ensure that the homes of their families, friends, neighbours, other workers and other residents of their communities are safe from the ravages of fire that can begin from any number of circumstances, including natural and human-made circumstances. Their dedication has to be recognized by this nation.
The exemption that the hon. member has proposed tonight is just one of the many ways in which we can recognize the valuable service of these fire-fighters and as I indicated as well the first-response personnel and perhaps throughout the community.
I received a letter from the hon. member for Haldi-mand-Norfolk regarding this motion some time ago. At that point it was very simple for him to convince me of the value of this motion. I just want to quote before concluding so that all members of this House can benefit from the words. The hon. member in his letter says: "Volunteer fire-fighters serve their municipalities with very little compensation. Generally they are given honorariums to cover out of pocket expenses while in attendance at emergencies, fires, training sessions, et cetera. I have no doubt that their service is worth every penny".
I agree entirely. In fact their service is worth a penny and a half or even two pennies now in 1993 terms and the government should recognize that. This is a very small measure that can show the appreciation of a grateful nation to a very dedicated group of people, men and women, in particularly rural communities but in other parts of Canada. I very much support the initiative that has been put forward here today.
May 5, 1993

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too wish to join this debate in supporting my colleague. I am happy to be able to second this motion which is before the House at the present time.
The subject matter we are debating this evening goes back some years. In fact I believe in July 1982 my colleague from South West Nova raised a similar issue on the floor of the House of Commons. Thereafter on January 19, 1983 our colleague from Brampton-Georgetown who happens to be this very day a distinguished member of the Crown, namely the Minister of State for Finance, made a similar argument to my colleague from Haldimand-Norfolk who has brought this issue before the House.
The subject matter is not foreign to the House. It is something that we have been apprised of for quite some time. I would hope at the end of may remarks, indeed after I hear from my colleague from Ontario, my colleague from Dartmouth and others who wish to speak, that perhaps there could be a disposition within the House in view of what has been previously said that the matter be referred to a committee for further examination. It does not commit any government or any future government to pursue this in any vigorous way, but at least it gives members of Parliament an opportunity to examine in greater detail.
For the record, I have a number of fire departments in my own constituency and I wish to list them. I think it important that I put on the record some of the volunteer fire associations and their auxiliaries which I have the pleasure of representing here in the Parliament of Canada: South Bar, New Victoria, New Waterford, Dominion, Reserve, Glace Bay, Donkin, Port Morien, Grand Lake Road, Sydney River, East Bay, Gabarus, L'Ardoise, Louisbourg, Tower Road, Main a Dieu, Mira Road, Marion Bridge, Albert Bridge, Chappel Island, Big Pond, East Bay, Birch Grove, Scotchtown, Grand River and I am sure there are one or two that I may have missed.
The importance of mentioning these is that they are self-contained in individual municipal units across my constituency which geographically is big. Population-wise it is not the size of my colleague's, the hon. member for Dartmouth. Nevertheless, members in those communities to which I have made reference hold in high regard
Private Members' Business
the fire department and the men and women who work in the fire department and more important who volunteer their service to those departments.
I want to say to the House that it is all well and good to say this is a costly measure. It is. That is why I think we have to look at it carefully and that is why I submit it must be referred to a committee for further examination.
The sense of security that many of these volunteer agencies give to our senior citizens in rural communities across this country is absolutely amazing. Not only are they called upon to fight major fires, but they are called upon to do other services for individuals, whether it be a chimney fire, a fire inside a home, a gas fire, a car fire, a grass fire which may be adjacent to a senior citizens' complex or to the residence of an elderly couple, which is very important.
It has an impact for the purposes of insurance. It also has an impact for the purposes of property taxation. If one has those kinds of facilities and amenities which are close by and particularly being volunteer, that will certainly add to the resale value of one's home.
The individuals who are involved in these volunteer fire departments need to have training, they have to go for courses and they have to be updated. They attend many charitable activities. In fact some of them are sponsored by individual fire departments. Of course, they have become over the years the centre for the community.
I realize that we are in a pinch in terms of expenditures by the Government of Canada. I think as a bare minimum we as a Parliament would do ourselves well if we allow this subject matter, as I am sure my colleague would want, to go before the appropriate committee of this House in order that we could fully examine in fact the costs that are associated with this, particularly when we look at some of the tax exemptions which are given to corporations.
I know the hon. member for Ontario will rise in his place and condemn all of those corporations that get tax exemptions, whether it be the SkyDome in Toronto or whether it be the boxes at the Montreal Forum or those special boxes that they are going to build at the Palladium for the Ottawa Senators. I know the hon. member opposite will want to get up and condemn them.

May 5, 1993
Private Members' Business
I am saying that there has to be a measure of fairness. Individuals who volunteer their time, who put their life at risk, who jeopardize their family life to give service to a volunteer fire department I believe are at least as a bare minimum deserving of this Parliament's greater examination of the subject matter which is now before it which is to give an increase in the exemption from $500 to $1,000 a year.
The exemption was changed in 1980 from $300 to $500. In effect we are living with a 13-year exemption. I am sure that if one were to take a calculator and figure it out that $500 after 13 years times the rate of inflation would not equal $500.
Hence I believe this is another reason the subject ought to be referred to the appropriate committee. In fact just the other day I was going to raise this matter with the Clerk who I know has a great interest in volunteer fire departments because he understands and appreciates the work that they do all across this land. In fact, Mr. Speaker, I am certain that you do as well.
I hope we could proceed in a non-partisan way. My colleague, who deserves a great deal of credit for having brought this motion before us, would like to have the subject matter referred to the appropriate committee to have a fuller examination. On the basis of the most simple and fundamental rule of law of the land, the rules of natural justice, namely fairness, could be applied to those men and women who serve in our communities, our volunteer fire department and their auxiliaries. We should examine this in greater detail.
I hope that the House can be seized of this issue in a non-partisan way as I am sure Canadians would want us to do. I hope we can resolve this favourably, not only for the individuals in question as referred to by my colleague, but also for the Government of Canada and indeed the Parliament of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the invitation that the hon. member for Cape Breton extended to me to condemn the boxes in the SkyDome. I will be happy to comment about those things, time permitting.
I am surprised that in his presentation condemning these terrible things that exist in the Skydome, he did not condemn the businessmen in Cape Breton on whose boats I happen to have had an opportunity to sail. These businessmen deduct their boats as a business expense against their operations in Cape Breton even though their income is not derived from those boats.
I wonder if the hon. member wanted me to include those particular boats in the condemnation to which he is referring. I have sailed on them. I suspect he has too. I will be interested, when he has a chance to comment again, to hear whether they are included. I will be interested also whether those lobsters which are being shipped from his riding to my riding consistently to help the fishermen of his community are deducted as an expense or does he no longer want them deducted so that they become more expensive in my riding. I would be interested in some comments from him on those matters when he has the chance of course.
We are not here to discuss those issues. We are here to discuss in this motion a very important issue, how fire-fighters are treated in Canada with the exemption that they have and should that exemption be increased from $500 to $1,000 a year. On the surface, it appears to be a very good motion and one that has merit.
The hon. member has cited the volunteer departments in his communities. I represent three communities, the towns of Ajax, Pickering and Whitby and all three of them heavily rely on the volunteer fire-fighters to augment the full-time force. Because they are much larger communities we have full-time forces. The fact of the matter is that without volunteers, the full-time forces could not deliver the services that are required in the community.
One of the things that I think is very fundamental to this in my community is the role of the business sector in dealing with the volunteers. In my community when a volunteer fire-fighter is called to duty, he or she has to leave their place of employment, assuming of course it happens during the hours that she or he is on duty.
In the community of Ajax that I live in, and I know the same thing applies in Whitby and Pickering, those business people say to the volunteers: "Leave your job,
May 5, 1993

no problem. It is important you go. We will continue to pay you while you are there fighting fires or doing the job of a fire-fighter on behalf of the citizens" of the communities I represent.
There is no doubt about the importance of volunteers.
I am certainly very familiar with it. We can talk about that life-saving value or the asset-saving value. I have had the experience, travelling across Canada as I did in my other capacity before I was elected going into towns to find an industry to which I was going to sell some steel.
Do you know where you could find out most easily where these businesses were located or get the directions to the street that you were looking for? You could just pull into the fire hall and ask the volunteer usually on duty who could say: Yes, sir, you are looking for the A-B-C street. You just go down here, turn left, turn right and that will take you right to the company that you are looking for.
Usually I found the volunteers could also tell me about some other companies in the community that were doing similar things. I found them to be a very good resource, all of it for free. Therefore no one is going to question just how important the volunteers are in the community.
The problem I see with the motion is that we are dealing with the volunteerism only of fire-fighters. Fire-fighters are obviously very worthy of the $500 deduction that they gain. For example, in many of the metropolitan cities and certainly in the region of Durham where I reside, we now have volunteer or auxiliary policemen, which is more how we describe them.
They do not rush out in quite the same capacity as regular police forces to deal with emergency situations, but sometimes they are out on the street participating in public functions representing the police department. The citizens who walk up to this policeman believes fully that they are talking to a policeman and not to just an auxiliary policeman. Therefore these people, although not necessarily serving right on the front line, are in many cases expected to do the same work.
Yet this resolution does not deal with the issue of those people who, in my opinion, are serving in a very vital role just as the volunteer fire-fighter is doing. I use that as one example of some of the other issues.
Private Members' Business
What we are talking about here is really a fundamental principle of the tax system. When one is paid cash for services or cash or goods in return for services rendered, volunteering if that can be the example, if it is an income or if it is to replace income one must pay tax on that.
What we are doing here is taking the back door approach. The one exception that exists is how we handle fire-fighters as it is. There are other volunteer groups that continuously raise this preferential treatment and want similar benefits. Again, the only benefit that exists is for fire-fighters.
It leads to the question asked by many charities that have appeared in the past before the finance committee of which I am a member which is: "Why do volunteers not get the breaks in the form of exemptions, deductions or tax credits for donating their time whether or not they receive an allowance?"
They argue that donating time is an important contribution made by donors of money and property. This is just as important and in fact in many instances more important. We just need to look at all the volunteer groups that exist in our ridings. Those groups could not function without volunteers.
There is the local baseball association, the hockey association, the ringette association, the Red Cross and the cancer society. The list just goes on and on of organizations in this country that simply could not function without volunteers.
There should be no doubt about the value of volunteers in Canada. The question is, do the volunteers in those organizations have the right to the same benefit as the volunteers in the fire department? That is not a question I am capable of answering, to be fair, but it is certainly a question that is asked by many organizations who appeared before the finance committee.
While I fully support the point that donations of time are as important as donations of money it does not necessarily follow that the tax treatment of these two types of contributions must be identical. In fact there are justifications against providing tax incentives for donations of time. I will take a few minutes to give some examples.
From a practical perspective there would be tremendous difficulty in determining how much time was given and how much this service was worth. Would the value of

May 5, 1993
Private Members' Business
time reflect the person's regular remuneration? Would it reflect the efforts put into the work done, or would it reflect the value to society? Even if the fundamental question of how to value the time could be resolved it would unfortunately not prevent the tremendous scope of abuse created by such a policy.
There is also the problem that stems from the fact that many volunteers are seniors and students, who would in many cases receive no tax deduction because they have no income. A deduction is only relevant if people have income. Having no income or an income that is so low they would receive no credits or deductions they would pay no taxes.
Philosophically it could be argued that any scheme to compensate individuals through the tax system for volunteer services would mean that volunteer services were no longer performed for free, but were paid for to a degree by the federal government. The federal government does not pay. It simply takes the money from taxpayers and gives it to someone else. This idea that the federal government pays is really an anomaly.
There is little evidence to indicate that offering enhanced tax assistance for volunteer activities would result in a significant increase in these services. Individuals volunteer for a number of reasons, most of which are unrelated to tax assistance. I come back to those volunteer firemen because I have had an opportunity to meet with many of them in my community. I do not think they are volunteer firemen for the money they receive or for the deduction of which they get to take advantage.
Many of us in this Chamber may have volunteered prior to our election and probably after our election still serve on many committees. We serve on those committees for many valuable reasons. First and foremost, we enjoy serving on those committees. There are many ways that we can give of our time. It is safe to say that we all move around and will ultimately give of our time in those places where we enjoy giving our time. Fortunately the advantage is that while we are giving our time somebody else is benefiting.
I believe that is the case with volunteer fire-fighters. I believe they enjoy what they are doing. Yes, it is very risky and they are very professional. They have to believe in what they are doing. However I do not believe this
motion will necessarily change the pros or cons of whether they should be or not be a fire-fighter.
As for the idea of referring this to a committee, I know that ultimately tax matters come to the finance committee of which I am a member. If members of the Liberal Party at any time want to raise that in committee as a subject for consideration they can do so. I do not believe we need to refer it to that committee from this House.

Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to commend the member for Haldimand- Norfolk for his persistence and diligence in pursuing this particular motion. I am going to speak to the substance of the motion.
I have seen some fancy footwork in the House of Commons on many occasions but I have to say that the speech from the member for Ontario was about the worst dance I have seen in here in a long time. The member for Ontario wants to get up and praise the work of the fire-fighters and volunteer fire departments, get his little political plug in for his firemen back home and then set about to completely misstate the intention of this motion.
I recognize that sometimes some of the backbenchers on the government side, the ones who do not get to get up to the front and probably never will, have to get up and say things in response to private members' motions that they may not believe. Sometimes they should stay home instead of coming here. After listening to what the hon. member just said I think this is one of those days when he probably would have been better off somewhere else.
He just does not get the point. He talked a lot about volunteers and he talked a lot about how can we say how much money a volunteer for the Cancer Society is worth. My mother has volunteered every year since I was a child for the Cancer Society. She goes out and canvasses all over the place. She does not do it looking for money. Neither are people who work for the Red Shield Appeal. I am the general chairman in the Halifax-Dartmouth area. I am not looking for a tax deduction. The member just does not get it.
To try to get wound up in words so he can explain away the fact that he does not support the motion or the very good suggestion by my colleague for Cape Breton-East
May 5, 1993

Richmond that this be referred to a committee for study shows that he really does not get it.
We are not talking about pitting one volunteer against another. We are not talking about a motion that is meant to entice people into working in volunteer fire departments. My god, the man just did not listen to what was said tonight.
We are talking about giving some due recognition by way of an increased tax exemption to members of volunteer fire departments. That is all we are talking about.
Let the record show that we are not talking about a new exemption. We do not need a debate as to whether or not firemen should get an exemption, which is what he tried to do. It is already there. It is $500. We heard that it was increased from $300 to $500 in 1980.
What my colleague from Haldimand-Norfolk simply says is that perhaps time and inflation have surpassed the $500 value mark that was given in 1980.
Let us remember when we talk about volunteer firemen, with the greatest respect for all the other volunteers in the community that build our communities and our neighbourhoods in our country, that volunteer firemen are quite different.
When my mother goes out and collects for the Cancer Society or when she goes because there is a problem at Lingan colliery or a disaster in the community she most likely does not have to worry about whether she is going to come home from that canvass. The men and women who work in volunteer fire departments have that worry every time that alarm rings.
When my mother goes out and canvasses for the Red Shield Appeal she does not have to worry about whether she will breathe in something that in 15 years time is going to cause some type of a cancer. Volunteer firemen and women do. She does not have to have her heart stop every time the phone rings. Volunteer firemen and women do.
To try to be all things to all people tonight and still spout the government line, which is a very tough line that says they do not deserve it and they are not going to get it but the government loves the job they do because
Private Members' Business
they are all electors and it has to count on their vote, is simply unbelievable.
I am very discouraged that this member, after serving a number of terms in this place, would try to pull such a stunt like that this evening this close to an election.
The member for Ontario has a great track record on supporting pieces of legislation or private members' bills and motions that recognize the unusual contribution that some people make to their community and their country.
The Remembrance Day bill was one the few bills that was passed here at second reading. It was a private member's bill, which I sponsored, to recognize the contributions of the men and women who have served in the Canadian Armed Forces. It was passed by this House. It was an unusual thing. The Tories even voted for it. The parliamentary secretary to the current defence minister, contender to the Tory throne, supported it.
This member, the member for Ontario, to show what a great supporter of those types of efforts he is, killed it at committee.
I was not totally surprised when he did his little fan dance around the issue as to whether or not he believes that volunteer firemen and women should get recognized for the work they do and the risks they take. I was not surprised but I was shocked with the way that he tried to pursue it.
If he does not want to give the exemption, if he wants to be the mouthpiece here, he should have just said it and then at least we could sit down and say that we know where he stands, but he had to dance around it.
The Ontario two-step.

The Ontario two-step.
On the motion itself, the member for Haldimand- Norfolk is quite correct. The contributions to communities that volunteer firemen and women make is unusual and unique. It is very unique.
He talked about the tire fire down in Hagersville. He talked about the efforts of those volunteer men and women at the fire department to try to protect their communities. They were working in situations where carcinogens were coming from the smoke. They did not know what they were breathing in but they did it because they are committed to the safety of their community.

May 5, 1993
Private Members' Business
They put the safety of the community and the benefit of people who they do not even know ahead of their own safety. They leave wives, husbands, sons, daughters, mothers and fathers at home. They go and put their lives on the line every single time that fire bell rings.
In my riding we have volunteer and full-time fire departments. They are supplemented by volunteer service in Eastern Passage, Cow Bay, Dartmouth and Westphal. The men and women who work at those stations are not just there each time the buzzer rings. They are there when there is a need to go into the schools and talk to the young kids about fire safety. They are there when the community needs assistance for a fund-raising drive or at the Eastern Passage-Cow Bay summer festival. They are always there. They give untiringly of themselves to build their communities.
This motion recommends something very simple. It is not telling the government we want to bankrupt it because it is pretty much bankrupt already. It is not telling the government we want to do something unusual, the principle of which has not been debated and discussed, because it has been. There is currently a firemen's tax exemption.
It says we recognize that this is a very special group of volunteers and as a Parliament there is very little we can do except increase the tax exemption. My friend from Cape Breton-East Richmond said that if we do our mathematics and take $500 in 1980 up to 1993 dollars and put the annual rate of inflation factor on that, we will probably give them the same exemption in constant dollars in 1993.
I find it disturbing that every time these types of issues come up members opposite find reasons not to do it. The last time an issue came up like this it dealt with radio licence fees and we debated it here in the House of Commons. There was a huge increase in radio licence fees.
Volunteer fire departments from across Canada signed petitions. They said that as volunteer fire departments they have to count on fund-raising activities. They have to go to the community to raise money for oxygen tanks and training because it is not always provided by the taxpayer. They have to go and squeeze it out.
When that issue came before the Parliament of Canada the members opposite said exactly the same thing: "Well, you know we think they do a great job but somebody has to pay for this", recognizing and knowing full well that the rhetoric was not only not supportable it was highly offensive to many people.
In conclusion I would like to once again commend my colleague from Haldimand-Norfolk for being persistent and diligent in giving the men and women who serve in volunteer fire departments right across this country the type of recognition they deserve on the floor of the House of Commons.

speechtext: I regret the hon. member's time has expired.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Shields (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to stand before the House today. I too want to go on the record as recognizing the volunteer fire department. I would also like to recognize the many other volunteers in our society. For example, there are a number of volunteers in each of our communities who are running food banks.
I have visited a number of the food banks where food is received and processed. It may not be as life-threatening as some of the work the firemen do sometimes, but to me it is every bit as rewarding. These volunteers with no pay whatsoever, no stipend, no equipment issued by the community to do their jobs as volunteers are there and often ruin their own clothing packing shelves with groceries, hauling around boxes and so on.
I think it is a real shame that this sort of thing happens. I heard it today because one of my colleagues stood up in the House and I thought gave a reasoned argument to the debate. His motives were questioned. He was told he had to speak the party line and he would never have the opportunity to sit in the front bench.
All kinds of nasty comments were directed at a colleague of mine who I feel has contributed a great deal in the way he goes about his work in committee, in the way he goes about his work in the House of Commons, and in the way he goes about treating all members in a very reasoned and thoughtful manner and with a great deal of respect.
May 5, 1993

I do not think it was called for. It is Private Members' Hour and a private member puts forward an idea or a motion knowing full well he is probably not going to get anywhere. However he does it for political reasons because it may give him some profile in his community among a certain group.
This is the anomaly we have in the situation. We treated firemen in this way back in the 1980s. By the way, all those groups came to governments in the past and said that this was what they wanted. They wanted the same treatment as was being given to volunteer fire departments or members of volunteer fire departments. Only the volunteer firemen received that kind of treatment from the tax department. If we were to readdress this anomaly with firemen, it would open the door to all other volunteer groups to be treated exactly the same way as volunteer firemen.
This may not sound very significant. One might ask: Why not allow them all to come in? However, at a time when volunteerism is becoming increasingly more important in our society, the cost of this alone could be a great deal of money. I have not been able to calculate it, but one has only to look at all volunteer organizations from the Canadian Cancer Society to my hon. friend's mother who does these kinds of things. I am not saying that his mother would seek this kind of support, but the organizations would.
We already have occasions of this. When we refer to the Unemployment Insurance Act, people on the opposite side of the House have said emphatically time and time again that we should allow people drawing unemployment insurance to work in volunteer organizations and at volunteer jobs. They should be able to work in the food banks and still draw unemployment insurance, even though the law states very clearly that these people must be available on a full-time basis for work.
This may not be a tremendous load to put on the Canadian public at this time, but it could lead to a tremendous load on the Canadian taxpayer. It would be a signal to every volunteer organization that they have exactly the same rights and should be treated in exactly
Private Members' Business
the same way irrespective of the jobs they do and irrespective of how we may look upon them as being special. All volunteers are special.
As I said, it is an anomaly. It has only been done to one group. If we readdress it, it opens the door for the others. Contrary to what my friends have said, other groups have come forward to the government and other groups have written in from their headquarters to say very clearly that they wanted to be treated in exactly the same way as the firemen were being treated under the tax situation.
